Psalm references follow the Vulgate numbering used in the edition. Stray footnote letters have been omitted. In XXVII the edition reads 'non enim ita nulla'; translated as 'nulla' (no increase suffices), and 'at gerendum' read as 'ac gerendum'. In XXI 'occulis' read as 'occultis'. In XXIII the edition reads 'quae ducit ad vitam' citing Matt. 7:13; the verse is 7:14.

Scanning errors read as evident: 'verae' as 'vere' (justly); 'debilis' as 'debitis' (due); 'openote' as 'operante'; 'viliorum' as 'vitiorum' (vices); 'judicaturus' taken as 'he who is to judge'. In XLIX the text is garbled ('bonus temporalibus... malis autem ideo a hujusmodi infelicitate 'initur'); read as 'malus autem ideo hujusmodi infelicitate punitur'. In XXXI the Latin shifts between third person (ascendunt) and first (profitemur); rendered as it stands. In XLIX 'properæ' read as 'prosperæ'. Reference 'lib. iv de Civ. v. 5' corresponds to City of God 4.3; given as 4.3.

LVIII: '.ottonum' read as 'motuum' (motions). LXIII: 'cumque' read as 'eumque'. LXXXI: 'quod corda concipitur' read as 'quod corde concipitur'. LXXXIV: 'excident' read as 'excidit'. LXXVI: 'reticet ejus gloriam' rendered with an implied verb.

Line 130 holds both the heading CXV (printed 'ex v.') and its maxim; translated together. Headings 'ex VI.' and 'CtI.' read as CXVI and CVI. In CXVII 'timere' read as 'timore' and 'quam..' as 'quamvis'. In CXXI 'bono' read as 'homo'. CXV 'fit de te magis quam facis': sense is that the deed is wrung from you rather than done by you. CXX cites 'Zephirin. ep. 1', apparently Pope Zephyrinus' (spurious) first letter; reference kept as printed.

Heading at ab127 printed 'CXIVIII. o te fide', read as CXXVIII 'De fide'; heading at ab145 printed 'CLVI', read as CXLVI. In 154, 'petas competeret esse eum Dee' read as 'potius competeret esse cum Deo'. In 146 'qui sanatur' read as 'quo'; in 148 'qua.' as 'quam'. Book references in the edition are garbled ('l. it', 'I. III'); given as City of God XI and XII by sequence.

CLXV: the Latin 'magis debent patres quod dominantur' lacks an expressed verb; 'to bear' is supplied from the parallel 'tolerare'. CLXXIV: 'DIU' is read as 'Deus'. CLXXV: the clause 'qui numquam a non dimittente amittitur' is compressed; Augustine's sense is that God is never lost except by one who forsakes him. Several source references in the printed text appear garbled (e.g. Civ. Dei XVIII c. i, XVI for XIX, Confess. book numbers); likely corrections have been given in the English, so readers comparing with the original will find some reference numbers changed.

Several 'Alias' numbers are misprinted in the scan (e.g. CLIXVIII, CLXXVII, CLXXVIII for CLXXXVII, CLXXXVIII); the evident sequence has been given. Ref 205 also contains the heading and text of CLXXXVII, and ref 220 combines heading CCII with its text, as in the source. In 205 'loquendi' read as 'loquenda'. In CXC 'qui hic discreverit causam suam' echoes Ps. 42:1 'discerne causam meam'; 'separated his cause' i.e. had it distinguished from that of the ungodly. In CCIV 'initiatur' may mean 'is consecrated/initiated'; rendered 'is founded'.

Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. nhi = nisi, Injus = hujus, LilII = LXIII, n. it = n. 11). In CCXI 'lumine poenitente' is read as 'homine poenitente' (man doing penance), which the sense requires. In CCXXIX the citation John 1:5 is as printed; the quotation is John 1:3. In CCXXXVI 'Nullus in Deo locus est' sits oddly with the heading ('every place is in God'); the text may be corrupt (perhaps 'nullus est locus' with 'in Deo' displaced), but it is translated as printed. The psalm reference in CCXIII (52) may be an error, given the surrounding references to Pss. 58–59.

Several scanning errors read as evident: 'minet' as timet (267), 'invenimur' as invenitur (268), 'propi- lium' as propitium (264), 'odoro' as odore (290), 'Cat. II, 21' as Gal. 2:21 (285). Stray footnote letters omitted.

Line 295: 'c. H' read as ch. 11. Line 309: 'nullo bono alieno' rendered 'no good other than himself' (lit. 'no alien good'). Heading ab278: the edition's 'Alias CCLXXII' is evidently a misprint for CCLXXXI. Line 299: 'aestimaC' read as aestimat.

CCXCIII: 'etiam notis' is read as 'etiam malis' (gifts bestowed even on the evil), and 'de pœnis majorum' as 'de poenis malorum' (from the punishments of the evil); both appear to be scanning errors, and the readings suit the antitheses of the passage. The opening quotes Psalm 110(111):2. CCLXXXVI: 'quam jns e poena' is read as 'quam justa poena'. CCXCI: 'deviari' is taken as 'devitari' (avoided).
Line 347: 'vii' read as 'vix' (hardly). Line 341 contains both the end of CCCVI and the heading of CCCVII, as the edition prints them under one reference.

Many scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. 'graitia', 'cxsequi', 'gntiis' for guttis, 'Chrislus', 'vermea'). In CCCXXXVII the closing clause 'ubi unum idemque est quo mens potest quantum potest' is obscure; rendered literally. The 'alias' number in the CCCXXX heading reads CCCXVIII, evidently for CCCXXVIII.

381: 'can. 25 conc. haut. II' read as canon 25 of the Second Council of Orange (Arausicanum II). 391: 'a quia .Meretur' read as 'quia videretur' (because it would be seen). 386: 'It' before 'ignorant' taken as a stray mark; the subject of 'ignorant' is unexpressed and rendered 'people'. 401: 'p quod dili- sit' read as 'quod diligit'.

CCCLXII: 'nec in eis inveniuntur cupiditatibus' is ungrammatical as printed; perhaps read 'cupiditates' ('nor are cupidities found in them'); translated loosely. CCCLXXI, last sentence: 'sic ei dedit vitam procedere de illo, sicut procedit et de ipso' is ambiguous; taken as the Father giving the Spirit to proceed from the Son as from himself.

Line 424 is badly garbled in the scan ('Hist descendut', 'cro', 'occidit ut .Meret'); read as 'nisi descendat ad nos', 'caro', 'non cecidit ut jaceret', 'Si descendentem'. Line 425: 'elaverit' read as 'creaverit'. Line 429: 'adveHitUr' read as 'advertitur', 'non sint' as 'non sinit'. Line 430: the heading for CCCLXXXIII stands at the start of this line in the edition; 'precare' read as 'peccare', 'hon coIit' as 'non cogit'. The last heading's number is misprinted (GGGLIXXIV); read CCCLXXXIV.

Several scanning errors read as evident: in 431 the final clause follows Augustine's 'quam vera non est' sense ('any more than it is true'); in 432 'si pa- I. ipse angelo rum' read as 'si panis ipse angelorum'; in 436 'bonum intimum' read as 'bonum infimum' (lowest good); in 439 'auctoritis' read as 'auctoritas'; in 441 'operæ luneis' read as 'operae lineis/lineamentis' (features of the work); in 442 'Mutius' read as 'utilius' and 'dalci' as 'dulci' (Horace, Ars Poetica 343). The Wisdom citations in 443 are actually Wis. 8:7, 8:16 and 8:17. Sentence CCCXCII lacks an Augustinian source reference and does not appear to be Augustine's.

Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'Banc' for 'Hanc', 'hnmo' for 'homo', 'Ahram' for 'Abram'). In 447 'orem' is read as 'opem' (help), 'I inceret' as 'vinceret'. In 448 'exaraturi' is read as 'exaratum'. The verse quotations are kept within their prose passages as the edition gives them.

nodes.text: THE ONE BOOK OF MAXIMS OF ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE, CULLED FROM THE WORKS OF ST. AUGUSTINE.
I. What true innocence is.

True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor another: for whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul. And no one sins against another without first sinning against himself (Aug. on Ps. 100:2; Prosper on the same psalm).
II. On loving men.
Men are to be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved; for it is one thing to love what they were made, another to hate what they do (Aug. on Ps. 100:5; Prosper on the same psalm).
III. On true eternity.

True eternity and true immutability exist only in the Godhead of the Trinity, for whom being what it is is everlasting: because its nature, lacking a beginning and needing no increase, admits no change, just as it admits no end. But creatures, even those to whom God has given or will give eternity, are not wholly free of every end, because they are not outside change, since there is an end for them, and a beginning in time, and movement in place, and that very change which is made for their own growth (Prosper on Ps. 101:18).
IV. On the patience of God.

The patience of God, by which he spares [men] when he is despised, spares [them] even when he is denied, and wills the life of the sinner rather than his death, is the granting of repentance and the offer of amendment: nor are any of his works empty of mercy, since he looks to man's good both with indulgence and with the scourge (Aug. on Ps. 102:8; Prosper on the same psalm).
V. On the vengeance of God.

The divine goodness is angry chiefly in this world for this reason, that it may not be angry in the world to come; and it mercifully applies temporal severity, so as not to inflict eternal vengeance justly (Prosper on Ps. 102:9).
VI. On the true praise of God.

The confession of one who blesses is true when the sound of mouth and heart is the same. But to speak well and live badly is nothing other than to condemn oneself with one's own voice (Prosper on Ps. 102:21).
VII. On the virtue of charity.
Love of God and of neighbour is the proper and particular virtue of the devout and the holy, while the other virtues can be common to both good and bad (Aug. on Ps. 103:5; Prosper on the same psalm).
VIII. On the apostolic teaching.

The apostolic teaching is so wholesome and so life-giving that, according to the capacity of those who use it, it leaves no one without a share in it: for whether little ones or great, weak or strong, they have in it what to be fed on and what to be filled with (Prosper on Ps. 103:11).
IX. On seeking God.

He who seeks God seeks joy. Let him seek, then, in such a way that he rejoices not in himself but in the Lord. For by drawing near to God his ignorance is enlightened and his weakness strengthened, and he is given both understanding by which to see and charity by which to burn (Prosper on Ps. 104:4).
X. On spiritual distaste.
Just as it is harmful to the body to be unable to take bodily food, so it is dangerous to the soul to feel distaste for spiritual delights (Prosper on Ps. 106:18).
XI. On the ends of the good and the wicked.
Those who tend toward not-being are never many. For what is so liable to fewness as that which is owed to perdition (Prosper on Ps. 106:59)?
XII. On the calmness of God's vengeance.

God does not crave the punishment of the guilty as though desiring to be sated with vengeance; but he decrees what is just with calm, and disposes it with an upright will, so that even the wicked are not out of order (Prosper on Ps. 108:5).
XIII. On good understanding.

He has good understanding who rightly understands what is to be done and does it. Otherwise understanding without action is like wisdom without fear, since it is written: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Prosper on Ps. 110:10).
XIV. On rest for one still living in the flesh.

Even in this life the soul that has been rescued from the death of unbelief has its rest, and abstains not from the works of righteousness but from the doing of iniquity: so that, living to God and dead to the world, it may rest in the peaceful calm of humility and meekness (Prosper on Ps. 114:8).
XV. On making vows to God.

Whoever considers well what he should vow to God and what he should pay in vowing, let him vow and render himself. This is required, this is owed. Let Caesar's image be rendered to Caesar, let God's image be rendered to God (Luke 20:25). But just as one must see what you offer and to whom you offer it, so one must also consider where you offer it: for there is no place for true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church (Prosper on Ps. 115:8).
XVI. On justice and grace.

There are two recompenses of justice, when either good is rendered for good or evil for evil. The third is the recompense of grace, when through regeneration evils are forgiven and good things are rendered. And so it is made plain that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. But that recompense of the wicked, by which evil is rendered for good, God does not know; and unless he rendered good for evil, there would be none to whom he might render good for good (Aug. Sermon 7 on Ps. 118; Prosper on the same psalm, 17).
XVII. On the citizens of the heavenly homeland.

Everyone who belongs to the heavenly city is a stranger in the world, and while he uses temporal life he lives in a foreign land, where amid many enticements and many deceits it is for few to know and love God, those for whom the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes (Ps. 18:9), so that they are deceived neither in the love of God nor in that of their neighbour (Prosper on Ps. 118:19).
XVIII. On overcoming the desire of the flesh.

There is no one whose soul the corruptible body and earthly dwelling do not weigh down (Wisd. 9:15). But one must strive that the desires of the flesh be overcome by the vigour of the spirit, and that the inner man, who always feels himself resisted, may always expect to be helped by divine aid (Prosper on Ps. 118:25).
XIX. On the narrow way of life.

Narrow is the way that leads to life (Matt. 7:13); and yet it is not run except with an enlarged heart: for the road of virtues, on which Christ's poor walk, is broad to the hope of the faithful, even if it is narrow to the vanity of unbelievers (Prosper on Ps. 118:35).
XX. On the reward of the Christian religion.

God is to be worshipped with such affection and desire that he himself is the reward of his worship: for he who worships God in order to gain something else rather than him does not worship God, but that which he longs to obtain (Aug. Sermon 11 on Ps. 118:6; Prosper on the same psalm, 36).
XXI. On not judging hidden things.

To judge rashly of the secrets of another's heart is a sin, and it is unjust to rebuke on suspicion one whose works are seen to be nothing but good; since of things unknown to man God alone is the just judge, who is also the true examiner (Zephyrinus, Letter 1; Prosper on Ps. 118:39).
XXII. On the help of God.

It is of divine gift when we both think rightly and keep our feet from falsehood and injustice. For as often as we do good, God works in us and with us that we may work (Prosper on Ps. 118:59; and canon 9 of the Council of Orange).
XXIII. On the sufferings of the saints.

By the just judgement of God, power is often given to sinners by which they may persecute his saints: so that those who are helped and led by the Spirit of God may become more illustrious through the exercise of toils (Prosper on Ps. 118:62).
XXIV. On knowledge of the good.

There is no true knowledge of the good unless it is grasped for this purpose, that it may be done: for he does not meditate profitably on the law of God who labours to hold in memory what he does not fulfil in action (Prosper on Ps. 118:71, 77).
XXV. On love of the law.
He who loves the law of God proves that in wicked men he hates what is against the law, not the men (Prosper on Ps. 118:113).
XXVI. On searching the commandments of God.
Only a quiet mind can search the commandments of God. So that religious study may be pursued, then, the quarrels of the malicious must be driven off (Prosper on Ps. 118:115).
XXVII. On making progress.

No one is so learned, no one so instructed, that he does not need light from above: for no increase of divine goods is so sufficient that there does not always remain something which the rational mind desires both to understand and to do (Prosper on Ps. 118:125).
XXVIII. On the twofold work of God.

If we consider all people together, some of whom are saved by mercy and others are justly condemned, all the ways of the Lord, that is, mercy and truth, are distinguished by their outcome. But if we look at the saints alone, these ways of the Lord are not told apart. For there truth is inseparable from mercy, and mercy from truth: because the blessedness of the saints comes both from the gift of grace and from the recompense of justice (Prosper on Ps. 118:151).
XXIX. On keeping peace.

It belongs to Christian perfection to be peaceable even with the enemies of peace, in hope of their correction, not in agreement with their malice: so that if they follow neither the example nor the exhortation of love, they may at least have no grounds for which they ought to hate us (Prosper on Ps. 119:7).
XXX. On God's guarding.

The Lord guards us from all evil, not so that we suffer nothing adverse, but so that the soul is not defiled by the adversities themselves. For when temptation is present, a kind of entry is made into that which assails us; and when the temptation is brought to an end with a good outcome, that is, without a wound to the soul, there is an exit from the depth of temporal toil to eternal rest (Prosper on Ps. 120:7).
XXXI. On the help of God.
None ascend to fellowship with the heavenly Jerusalem except those of us who profess with our whole heart that it is not of their own work but of God's gift that they ascend (Prosper on Ps. 121:4).
XXXII. On the hatred of the world for Christians.

All who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer reproaches from the ungodly and from those unlike them, and be despised as foolish and mad, as people who lose present goods and promise themselves invisible and future ones. But this contempt and mockery will be turned back upon the ungodly, when both their abundance has passed into want and their pride into confusion (Prosper on Ps. 122:5).
XXXIII. On the patience of the faithful.

The whole salvation of the faithful, the whole strength of their patience, must be referred to him who is wonderful in his saints: because unless the Lord were in them, human frailty would succumb to the fury of the ungodly (Prosper on Ps. 123:5).
XXXIV. On due obedience.

Rulers are to be borne by the people, and masters by slaves, in such a way that temporal things are endured under the exercise of forbearance, and eternal things are hoped for. For it increases the merits of virtue that it does not violate the commitment of religion (Prosper on Ps. 124:3).
XXXV. On bearing the changeableness of the world.

The upright in heart do not complain about the precepts and ordinances of God: because it is right that all things be accepted with equanimity which he who is to judge has willed to be endured (Prosper on Ps. 118:4).
XXXVI. On the building of the house of God.

The whole standing of the holy building, just as it advances by God's working, so it endures by God's guarding. For the guarding of those set over [the people] is useful only when the Spirit of God presides over his people, and deigns to guard not only the flocks but also the shepherds themselves (Prosper on Ps. 126:1).
XXXVII. On eternal joys.

The joys of the eternal city are eternal, and the everlasting infinity of days that stand still will neither vary nor slip away: because they will possess an unchangeable peace, for whom the good of all will be what is also the good of each (Prosper on Ps. 127:5).
XXXVIII. On the law of charity.

The law of Christ is the perfection of charity, by which God and neighbour are loved, and through which it is said to the Founder of the law: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. (Matt. 6:12.) For he rightly awaits God's promise who carries out his commandments; nor does he hope in vain that his sins will be spared who pardons those of others (Prosper on Ps. 129:4).
XXXIX. On the commands of God.

God commands nothing that profits himself, but [only] the one whom he commands. Therefore he is the true Lord, who does not need a servant, and whom the servant needs (Aug. Letter 138, to Marcellinus, §6).
XL. On God's timeless knowledge.
What is new in time is not new with God, who founded the times, and holds without time all things which he distributes to their several times, according to their variety (Aug. ibid., §7).
XLI. On the providence of God.

An unchangeable reason contains the ordering of changeable things, where, without time, those things are together which do not happen together in time, because times do not run together (Aug. ibid., §8).
XLII. On the impunity of sinners.
Nothing is more unhappy than the happiness of sinners, by which a penal impunity is nourished, and an evil will, like an enemy within, is strengthened (Aug. ibid., §14).
XLIII. On the letter of the law.

The letter of the law, which teaches that one must not sin, kills if the life-giving Spirit is absent. For it causes sin to be known rather than avoided, and therefore increased rather than diminished; because to evil desire is added also the transgression of the law (Aug. On the Spirit and the Letter 5.14).
XLIV. On law and grace.

The law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled. For it was not through its own fault that it was not fulfilled, but through the fault of the prudence of the flesh: a fault which was to be shown through the law, and healed through grace (Aug. ibid., ch. 19).
XLV. On the promise of God.

God promises what he himself does. For he does not promise while another does it: that would no longer be promising but predicting. Therefore [it is] not from works but from him who calls (Rom. 9:12; and 4:4); lest it be theirs and not God's, and the reward be reckoned not according to grace but according to debt; and so grace would no longer be grace (Aug. ibid., ch. 24).
XLVI. On the faults of the faithful and the good deeds of unbelievers.

Just as certain venial sins, without which this life is not lived, do not keep the righteous from eternal life, so some good works, without which the life of even the worst person is very rarely found, are of no use to the ungodly for eternal salvation (Aug. ibid., ch. 27).
XLVII. On the effect of an evil will.

When an evil will receives the power to accomplish what it desires, this comes from the judgement of God, with whom there is no injustice. For he punishes in this way too: nor is it unjust because it is hidden. But the wicked man does not know he is being punished, unless through open punishment he feels unwillingly how much evil there is in what he committed willingly (Aug. ibid., ch. 31).
XLVIII. On pride.
All vices have force only in evil deeds: pride alone must be guarded against even in deeds rightly done (Aug. On Nature and Grace, ch. 27).
XLIX. On the unequal use of fortune.

It matters very much what use is made both of the things called prosperous and of those called adverse. For the good man is neither lifted up by temporal goods nor broken by temporal ills; but the bad man is punished by misfortune of this kind precisely because he is corrupted by good fortune (Aug. City of God 1.8).
L. On the death of the saints.

A death should not be thought bad which a good life has preceded. For nothing makes death bad except what follows death. So those who must necessarily die should not be much concerned with what befalls them so that they die, but with where they are compelled to go by dying (Aug. ibid., ch. 11).
LI. On purity, which one does not lose against one's will.

Thus holiness of body is not lost while holiness of mind remains, even when the body is overpowered; just as holiness of body is lost when purity of mind is violated, even if the body is untouched (Aug. ibid., ch. 18).
LII. On the fortitude of endurance.

That spirit is rightly called greater which chooses to bear a life of hardship rather than flee it, and, in the light and purity of conscience, to despise human judgement, and above all that of the crowd, which is for the most part wrapped in the darkness of error (Aug. ibid., ch. 22).
LIII. On free servitude and servile lordship.

For the just, whatever evils are inflicted by wicked masters are not a punishment for crime but a testing of virtue. For the good man, even if he is a slave, is free; but the bad man, even if he reigns, is a slave; and not of one man, but, what is worse, of as many masters as he has vices (Aug. City of God 4.3).
LIV. On the offering of vows.
No one would rightly vow anything to the Lord unless he received from him what he would vow (Aug. City of God 17.4, and canon 11 of the Second Council of Orange).
LV. On the essence of the Godhead.

Every substance that is not God is a creature, and what is not a creature is God. There is therefore no difference [of rank] in the Godhead of the Trinity, since what is less than God is not God (Canon 12 of the Second Council of Orange).
LVI. Of what kind are those whom God loves.
God loves us as we shall be by his gift, not as we are by our own merit.
LVII. On the timeless work of God.
The order of times is without time in the eternal wisdom of God, and nothing is new with him who made the things that are to be.
LVIII. On the principal cause of all things.

The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily and spiritual motions. For nothing happens visibly and perceptibly that is not either commanded or permitted from the invisible and intelligible court of the supreme Ruler, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments, of graces and recompenses, in this most ample and immeasurable commonwealth, as it were, of the whole creation (Aug. On the Trinity 3.4).
LIX. On the pride of the devil and the humility of Christ.

The proud devil led proud man to death; the humble Christ led obedient man back to life. For just as the one, being lifted up, fell and cast down the one who consented, so the other, being humbled, rose and raised up the one who believes (Aug. On the Trinity 4.10).
LX. On spiritual growth.

In spiritual things, when the lesser cleaves to the greater, as the creature to the Creator, the former becomes greater than it was, not the latter; and here to be greater is to be better, since the creature cleaving to the Creator becomes greater not by being larger in bulk but in power (Aug. On the Trinity 6.8).
LXI. On the ineffable excellence of the Godhead.

The surpassing eminence of the Godhead exceeds not only the power of our speech but also that of our understanding. For God is thought of more truly than he is spoken of, and he is more truly than he is thought of. And it is no small part of knowledge if, before we can know what God is, we can know what he is not (Aug. On the Trinity 8.2).
LXII. On true happiness.

All the happy have what they want, although not all who have what they want are therefore happy. But those are at once wretched who either do not have what they want, or have what they do not rightly want. A right will, then, even if it has not obtained what it desires, is nearer to happiness than a perverse one, even if it has got what it desires (Aug. On the Trinity 13.5).
LXIII. What it is to be with God.

It is a great misery for a man not to be with him without whom he cannot be. For he in whom he is, he is without doubt not without; and yet if he does not remember him, and does not understand him, nor love him, he is not with him (Aug. On the Trinity 14.12).
LXIV. On the incarnation of the Word of God.

The divinity of the Word, equal to the Father, was made a sharer in our mortality, not from what was his but from what was ours, so that we too might be made sharers in his divinity, not from what is ours but from what is his (Aug. on Ps. 118, sermon 16.6; and sermon 19.6).
LXV. With what hatred the wicked are to be hated.

Perfect hatred is that which lacks neither justice nor knowledge: that is, that you neither hate men on account of their vices nor love vices on account of men. Rightly, then, in the wicked we hate the wickedness and love the creature, so that neither is the nature condemned on account of the vice, nor the vice loved on account of the nature (Aug. City of God 14.6; Prosper on Ps. 138:22).
LXVI. On the toil of those who invent lies.

The inventions of falsehood are difficult and toilsome. But he who wishes to speak the truth does not toil; for the good are more at rest than the wicked, and the words of the truthful are more straightforward than the fabrications of deceivers (Aug. on Ps. 139.13).
LXVII. On the divine Scriptures.

Good are the depths of the mysteries in the holy Scriptures, which are hidden for this reason, that they may not become cheap; are sought for this reason, that they may exercise [us]; and are opened for this reason, that they may feed [us] (Aug. on Ps. 140.1).
LXVIII. On the prayer of the Lord.
The Lord Jesus Christ, praying with bloody sweat, signified that the sufferings of the martyrs would flow forth from his whole body, which is the Church (Aug. ibid., 4; and on Ps. 85.1).
LXIX. On receiving the sacraments.
The unworthy man takes the sacrament of godliness to his own judgement. For what is good cannot be good for one who receives it badly (Aug. on Ps. 142.16).
LXX. On praising God.

He who praises God in the wonders of his benefits praises him also in the terrors of his vengeance. For he both coaxes and threatens. If he did not coax, there would be no encouragement; if he did not threaten, there would be no correction (Aug. on Ps. 144.8; Prosper on the same psalm, 5).
LXXI. On hastening conversion.

The remedies of conversion to God are not to be put off by any delays, lest the time for correction be lost through slowness. For he who promised pardon to the penitent did not pledge tomorrow to the one who disregards [it] (Aug. ibid., 11).
LXXII. On humility in praying.

He is upright and calls rightly upon God who in all the evils he suffers accuses himself, not God, and in the good things he does praises not himself but God. For just as God repels the one who defends his sins, so he receives the one who confesses them (Aug. ibid., 12).
LXXIII. On wonder at created things.

Wonderful is the structure of the world, but more wonderful its maker. And he who departs from the Creator is wrongly occupied with created things; but if he cleaves to the higher, he will trample on the lower, lest what he has loved against nature be turned into punishment (Aug. on Ps. 145.5).
LXXIV. On the disordered soul.
The rational soul that puts lower things before higher cannot rule what it used to rule, because it refused to be ruled by him by whom it was ruled (Aug. ibid., 5).
LXXV. On the punishment of sin.
The body of our flesh was an ornament to us: we sinned, and from it we received fetters, so that the whole course of human actions is hampered by the chains of mortality (Aug. ibid., 17).
LXXVI. On the right way of singing psalms.

He sings rightly in praise of God whose works agree with his voice. For when the song is finished, the voice falls silent; but a life persevering in good deeds never ceases [to proclaim] the glory of him whom it rejoices to see working in it (Aug. on Ps. 146.2).
LXXVII. On fear.
All things that are feared are reasonably avoided: God is to be feared in such a way that one flees from him to him (Aug. ibid., 20).
LXXVIII. On right anxiety.
Just as misplaced security drives into danger, so well-ordered anxiety gives birth to security (Aug. on Ps. 147.5).
LXXIX. On virginity.
Virginity of the flesh: an untouched body; virginity of the soul: uncorrupted faith (Aug. ibid., 10).
LXXX. On the manner of possessing.

We shall be shown to have many superfluous things among our possessions if we keep only what is necessary. For to those who seek vain things nothing is enough, and he is in a way a withholder of what belongs to others who uselessly keeps what would benefit the poor (Aug. sermon on Ps. 147.12; Prosper on Ps. 144:5).
LXXXI. On thoughts.

As our ears are to our voices, so are God's ears to our thoughts. But it cannot happen that good thoughts issue in evil works, since what is conceived in the heart is brought out in action (Aug. on Ps. 148.2).
LXXXII. On the new song.

Just as the old song of the old man pertains to temporal things, so the new song of the new man pertains to eternal things; and so each one sings as he lives. Now the new song is the song of faith that works through love (Aug. on Ps. 149.1).
LXXXIII. On true humility.

The true humility of the faithful is to be proud in nothing, to murmur at nothing; to be neither ungrateful nor complaining, but in all God's judgements to give thanks to God and to praise God, all of whose works are either just or kind.
LXXXIV. On those without hope.

Exceedingly wretched is he who does not hope in God and promises himself success from himself, since by the very fact that he does not seek God's help he falls away from all hope of true salvation (Aug. on Ps. 33, exposition 2.13).
LXXXV. On riches.

Those who are rich from iniquity are in great want; they do not have the wealth of justice and the treasures of wisdom. But those who serve the Lord acquire those goods that cannot perish (Aug. ibid., 15).
LXXXVI. On true goodness.
It is not enough to abstain from evil unless what is good is done; and it is little to harm no one unless you strive to benefit many (Aug. ibid., 19).
LXXXVII. On the impunity of evil.

The sinner who sins is not therefore unseen by the Lord because the punishment of the one who does evil is deferred; but a heavier sentence is decreed against him to whom even correction itself is denied (Aug. ibid., 21).
LXXXVIII. On the good of humility.
The height of God is not approached except through humility; and the one to whom the submissive draws near, the proud withdraws far from (Aug. ibid., 23).
LXXXIX. On burial.
Just as sumptuous funerals do no good to rich sinners, so mean burials, or none at all, do no harm to poor saints (Aug. ibid., 25).
XC. On right joy.
He whose joy is Christ can never be cheated of his delights. For that rejoicing is eternal which delights in an eternal good.
XCI. What joins a human being to God.
To God, who is everywhere, we are either far or near not by places but by actions: for as unlikeness separates [us], so imitation joins us to him (Aug. on Ps. 34, 6).
XCII. On the good battle.

It belongs to human sickness to take delight in sinning in mortal flesh. But the disciple and lover of virtues ought not to grant peace to this concupiscence, but to declare war [on it] (Aug. on Ps. 35, 6).
XCIII. On the hope of the faithful.

Do not let it frighten you, Christian, that the things believed are deferred: although the promise is hidden, let prayer nevertheless persevere in hope. Exercise yourself in works, grow in virtues. While the constancy of faith is tested, the glory of recompense is increased.
XCIV. On the times of the wicked.
All the time of the wicked is short. For what is so slight as that which tends toward this: not to be?
XCV. On the increase of charity.
The resources of charity always grow, since by use it becomes greater, and by generosity richer.
XCVI. On the passing away of the wicked.
The impiety of the wicked must perish, either by their own judgement or by the sentence of God. For no iniquity endures; correction or damnation puts an end to it.
XCVII. How one cleaves to God.
One who cleaves to God and always does his will is never deserted by his indweller: and if he suffers certain hard and adverse things, he is not abandoned, but tested.
XCVIII. On justice.

The whole principle of justice is that evils be shunned and goods be done: the pattern of this observance must be kept amid any adversities whatever, because this alone is never lost, which is spent on the work of piety.
XCIX. On endurance.

Let present evils be endured until the promised beatitude comes. Let the unbelievers be borne with by the faithful, and let the uprooting of the tares that have sprung up among the wheat be deferred. However much the impious rage, the cause of the just is better even in this time; the more fiercely they are attacked, the more gloriously they are crowned (Aug. Sermon 3 on Ps. 36, 17).
C. What the cry to God is.

The cry to God is the intent of the heart and the ardour of love; for what is always desired is always asked for. And this is not hidden from God, since what proceeded from him returns to him (Aug. on Ps. 38, 14).
CI. On confessing sin.
Confession of sin is good if healing follows. For what use is it to uncover the wound and not apply medicine (Aug. ibid., 24)?
CII. On perfection.
In this life, which is wholly temptation, even in the most sublime saints, that perfection is not attained beyond which no ascent remains.
CIII. On the labours of the present life.

While the course of the present life is being run, even if a man advances greatly whose outer self is being corrupted and inner self renewed, it is nevertheless necessary that, while he is subject to the condition of death, he endure the labours of the old state (Aug. on Ps. 38, 8 and 9).
CIV. That the human being is the image of God, now subject to vanity.

The human being is indeed the image of God, and [so is] he who walks in the ways of justice and strives toward the likeness of his maker; and yet while he lives in this life he meets the disturbances of vanity (Aug. ibid., 11).
CV. On divine instruction.

The first grace of the divine gift is that it instructs us to confess our lowliness, and makes us recognize that if we do anything good, we are able to through him without whom we can do nothing (Aug. ibid., 18).
CVI. That the whole life of unbelievers is sin.
The whole life of unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good without the highest good. For where knowledge of the eternal and unchangeable truth is lacking, virtue is false, even in the best morals.
CVII. On the spiritual foundation.

Just as the foundation of a bodily building is at the bottom, so the foundation of the spiritual building is at the top. Earthly building begins from the earth; heavenly construction grows from a beginning on high.
CVIII. That remembering or forgetting do not apply to God.

God is said to remember when he acts, and to forget when he does not act. For neither does forgetting apply to God, since he is in no way changed, nor remembering, since he forgets nothing (Aug. Enarr. on Ps. 87, 5).
CIX. Who see the wonders of God.
Those see the wonders of God whom they benefit. For what is not understood, or from which no profit is gained, is not seen (Aug. ibid., 10).
CX. On joining mercy and truth.

Let truth not take away mercy, nor mercy hinder truth. For if for mercy's sake you judge against truth, or through rigid truth, as it were, you forget mercy, you will not walk in the way of the Lord, in which mercy and truth have met each other (Aug. Sermon 1 on Ps. 88, 25).
CXI. On the temptation and imitation of Christ.

The temptation of Christ is the instruction of the Christian. For disciples ought to be imitators of the master, not in working miracles, which no one demands, but in keeping humility and patience, to which the Lord invited us by his example (Aug. Sermon 1 on Ps. 90).
CXII. On cupidity and charity.
As cupidity is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all goods (Aug. ibid., 8).
CXIII. On the joy of the Christian.

For the Christian the cause of rightly rejoicing is not the present age but the future one; and temporal things are to be used in such a way that they do not stand in the way of eternal ones, so that on the road on which pilgrims walk, that may please [them] which leads to the homeland.
CXIV. On the sabbath.
He keeps the sabbath badly who rests from good works. But rest from iniquity ought to be perpetual, because a good conscience makes [one] not restless but tranquil (Aug. Enarr. on Ps. 91, 2).
CXV. That good is to be done with joy. When you do good, do it cheerfully. For if you do anything good gloomily, it is done from you rather than you doing it (Aug. Enarr. on Ps. 91, 5).
CXVI. That not men, but men's perversity, is to be shunned.

If the good do not pass over into the ways of the wicked, there is a great division even among those who live together. Therefore it is not men, who can be corrected by the example of better men, but men's iniquity that is to be shunned.
CXVII. That sins are to be avoided not from fear of punishment but from love of justice.

God approves that innocence by which a man becomes innocent not from fear of punishment but from love of justice. For he who does not sin from fear, although he does not harm the one he wishes to harm, yet harms himself very greatly; and though abstaining from the wicked deed, he is nevertheless guilty by his will alone (Aug. Enarr. on Ps. 93, 1).
CXVIII. On humble confession and proud boasting.
Confession in bad deeds is better than proud boasting in good ones (Aug. ibid., 15).
CXIX. That the malice of the wicked benefits the good.
By the malice of the wicked the good man is scourged; and by the servant the son is corrected (Aug. ibid., 25).
CXX. On the perseverance of the faithful.

Just as night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly iniquity does not darken the minds of the faithful who cleave to the firmament of holy Scripture (Zephyrinus, Ep. 1; Aug. Enarr. on Ps. 93, 29).
CXXI. On man's own capacity.
For sinning man is abundantly supplied by his own capacity; but for doing good he is not sufficient for himself, unless he is justified by him who alone is just (Aug. Enarr. on Ps. 98, 7).
CXXII. On contrary ways of life.

It is a great labour for the good to endure contrary ways of life; whoever is not offended by them makes little progress. For another's iniquity torments the just man as much as he withdraws from his own (Aug. ibid., 12).
CXXIII. How one approaches God or withdraws from God.

God is not approached or withdrawn from by distances of place; but likeness makes [one] near, unlikeness far. And it is the greatest misery to be far from that good which is everywhere (Aug. Enarr. on Ps. 99, 5).
CXXIV. On true freedom.
Service with God is always free, for it is not necessity that serves him but charity (Aug. ibid., 7).
CXXV. On tolerance.

Whoever is willing to bear with no one because, as he supposes, he has made great progress, shows by the very fact that he does not tolerate others that he has rather made no progress (Aug. ibid., 9).
CXXVI. Where our good comes from.

All the good that we have, we have from our maker. But if what is in us is what we ourselves have made, we shall be condemned for it; if it is what God has made, we shall be crowned for it (Aug. ibid., 15).
CXXVII. On the Incarnation of the Word.

The Word of God, through whom all things were made, foreordained the time at which he would take up flesh; he did not yield to time so as to be turned into flesh. For man came to God; God did not withdraw from himself (Aug. Ep. 137, 10).
CXXVIII. On faith and understanding.
Faith opens the way to understanding; unbelief closes it (Aug. ibid., 15).
CXXIX. On pride.

The vice by which man was first overcome is the last that he overcomes. For when he has overcome all sins, the danger remains that the mind, conscious of its own good, may glory in itself rather than in the Lord (Aug. Enarr. on Ps. 7, 4).
CXXX. On the fulfilment of desires.

The end of cares is the fulfilment of desires; and each person strives and struggles towards this, to arrive at that in which he delights. It is therefore the part of the wise man to seek what makes [him] good, not to love what deceives (Aug. ibid., 9).
CXXXI. On the two gifts of grace.

Just as there are two tasks of medicine, one by which sickness is healed, the other by which health is preserved, so there are two gifts of grace, one which takes away the cupidity of the flesh, the other which makes the virtue of the soul persevere (Aug. ibid., 10).
CXXXII. On the end of labour.
A man's labour cannot be ended unless he loves what cannot be taken from him (Aug. ibid., 16).
CXXXIII. On the harm done by iniquity.
It is impossible for iniquity to harm the just man at whom it aims before it harms the unjust heart from which it proceeds (Aug. ibid., 17).
CXXXIV. On visible and invisible miracles.

A visible miracle calls to illumination; an invisible one illuminates him who has been called and has come. So he tells all the wonders of God who, believing the visible, has made the passage to understanding the invisible (Aug. Enarr. on Ps. 9, 2).
CXXXV. On those who flee the devil.

Better is the case of those who flee the devil as he pursues them than of those who follow him as he goes before, because it is more profitable to have him as an enemy than as a leader (Aug. ibid., 4).
CXXXVI. On depraved cupidities.

All depraved cupidities are the gates of hell, through which one goes into death; he comes under its dominion who rejoices that he has obtained, for full enjoyment, what he has desired in a way that leads to perdition (Aug. ibid., 14).
CXXXVII. On flattery.
The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins: for it is pleasant to do those things in which not only is no reprover feared, but even a praiser is heard (Aug. ibid., 21).
CXXXVIII. On a mind conscious of evil.

A mind conscious of its own evil, while it seems to itself to suffer no punishment, believes that God does not judge; whereas to abuse God's patience, and not to understand the kindness of one who spares, is already a great condemnation (Aug. ibid., 23).
CXXXIX. That nature is prior to vice.

In a creature that sins by its own choice, nature is prior to vice; and vice is so contrary to nature that it can only harm nature. So withdrawing from God would not be a vice unless it rather befitted the nature whose vice this is to be with God (Aug. City of God XI, 17).
CXL. On evil angels and men.

God would not create any angel or man whom he foreknew would be evil, unless he likewise knew to what good uses he would put them, and so would adorn the order of the ages, like a most beautiful poem, even with certain antitheses (Aug. ibid., 18).
CXLI. On the creation of the creature.

Three things above all, which we needed to know about the creation of the creature, had to be made known to us: who made it, through what he made it, why he made it. God said, it says, Let there be light, and there was light; and God saw the light, that it was good (Gen. 1:3). So if we ask who made it: it is God. If through what he made it: He spoke, and it was made. If why he made it: because it is good. There is no author more excellent than God, no art more effective than the word of God, no cause better than that good should be created by the good (Aug. ibid., 21).
CXLII. On good and evil love.

There is a love by which even what ought not to be loved is loved; and he hates this love in himself who loves that [love] by which what ought to be loved is loved. For both can be in one man, and this is good for man, that as the one by which we live well advances, the other by which we live ill should decline, until all that we live is healed to perfection and changed into good (Aug. ibid., 28).
CXLIII. On the good of the creature.

The good of a rational or intellectual creature, by which it is blessed, is nothing but God; and this it has not from itself, since it was created from nothing, but from him by whom it was created. For when this is gained it becomes blessed; when it is lost, wretched (Aug. City of God XII, 1).
CXLIV. On the vice of a nature.

Vice cannot exist in the highest good, nor except in some good. So good things alone can exist somewhere, but evil things alone nowhere. For even those natures that have been vitiated from the beginning of an evil will are evil in so far as they are vicious, but good in so far as they are natures (Aug. City of God XII, 3).
CXLV. That there is in God neither idle leisure nor laborious industry.

It is not right to believe that God is affected one way when he is at rest and another way when he works, for he should not even be said to be affected, as though something came about in his nature that was not there before. For whoever is affected undergoes something, and everything that undergoes is changeable. So let neither idle leisure nor laborious industry be thought of in God, for he knows how to act while resting and to rest while acting; and what is earlier or later in his works is to be referred not to the maker but to the things made. For his will is eternal and unchangeable, and is not varied by shifting counsel; in it is present at once whatever, in the creating or ordering of things, has gone before or follows (Aug. ibid., 17).
CXLVI. That God alone is creator.

No one may believe or say that anyone but God is the creator of any nature, however small. For even if angels, commanded or permitted, apply their working to things that are brought forth in the world, they are no more creators of animals than farmers are of crops and trees (Aug. ibid., 24).

CXLVII. On the first and second death of the body. Of the first death of the body it can be said that it is good for the good and evil for the evil. But the second, without doubt, just as it belongs to none of the good, so is good for none (Aug. City of God XIII, 2).
CXLVIII. On the death of the godly.

The death even of the godly is a punishment for sin. But it is called good for them because they use it well, for them it is an end to temporal evils and a passage to eternal life. For just as injustice uses ill not only evil things but also good ones, so too justice uses well not only good things but also evil ones (Aug. ibid., 5).
CXLIX. On unbaptized martyrs.

Those who die for the confession of Christ even without having received the washing of regeneration, it avails them as much for the abolishing of sins as if they were washed in the font of baptism (Aug. ibid., 7).
CL. That one must live not according to man but according to God.

When man lives according to himself, not according to God, he is like the devil, for neither should the angel have lived according to the angel but according to God, so as to stand in the truth and speak the truth from what is God's, not a lie from what is his own. Hence it is not said in vain that every sin is a lie, for there is no sinning except by that will which is contrary to truth, that is, to God (Aug. City of God XIV, 4).
CLI. On the diversity of human affection.

The diversity of human affection comes from the diversity of the will: if this is depraved, [the affection] will be restless with perverse habits; but if it is right, a man's affection will be not only not blameworthy but even praiseworthy (Aug. ibid., 6).
CLII. On true freedom of choice.

The choice of the will is truly free when it is not a slave to vices and sins. Such [a choice] was given by God, and once lost it cannot be restored except by him by whom it could be given. Hence the Truth says, If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free (Aug. ibid., 11).
CLIII. That the heart must be held toward God.

It is good to have the heart lifted up, yet not toward oneself, which belongs to pride, but toward God, which belongs to obedience. But by desiring more, he becomes less who, while trusting that he is sufficient for himself, falls away from him who truly suffices for him (Aug. ibid., 13).
CLIV. On the blessed life.

The blessed life, if it is not loved, is not possessed. Further, if it is loved and possessed, it must be loved more excellently than all other things, since whatever else is to be loved is to be loved for its sake. And since no one can be blessed except one who loves it as it deserves, it follows that he wills it to be eternal; for it will be truly blessed only when it has no end (Aug. ibid., 25).
CLV. That no one becomes good except from [being] evil.
Not all the wicked, indeed, advance so far as to become good; yet no one is good except from [having been] evil (Aug. City of God XV, 1).

CLVI. On the citizens of the earthly and the heavenly city. The citizens of the earthly city are born of nature vitiated by sin; these are vessels of wrath. But the citizens of the heavenly homeland are born of grace, which frees nature from sin; these are vessels of mercy (Aug. ibid., 2).
CLVII. On the wrath of God.

The wrath of God is not a disturbance in him, but the judgement by which punishment is inflicted on sin. And his thinking and rethinking is the unchangeable reason of things that are to be changed. For God does not repent of any deed of his as a man does (1 Kings 15:29), since his judgement concerning absolutely all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain (Aug. ibid., 25).
CLVIII. On those who persecute the Church.

The enemies of the Church, by whatever error they are blinded or by whatever malice depraved, if they receive power to afflict [her] bodily, exercise her patience; if they oppose her only by thinking wrongly, they exercise her wisdom; and so that even enemies may be loved, they exercise her benevolence: for God works all things together for good for those who love him (Aug. City of God XVIII, 51).
CLIX. On the end of good and of evil.

The end of good is not that by which it is consumed so as not to be, but that by which it is perfected so as to be full. And the end of evil is not that by which it ceases to be, but that to which it leads by doing harm. Hence the one is the highest good, the other the highest evil: the former, that for whose sake the other goods are to be sought, while it is [sought] for its own sake; the latter, that for whose sake the other evils are to be avoided, while it [is avoided] for its own sake (Aug. City of God XIX, 1).
CLX. On nature.
There is a nature in which there is no evil, or even in which no evil can be. But there cannot be a nature in which there is no good (Aug. ibid., 13).
CLXI. On equanimity of mind.
Equanimity of mind is better than health of body; and it is more fitting that the unjust man grieve in punishment than that he rejoiced in wrongdoing (Aug. ibid.).
CLXII. On the precept of charity.

In the precept of charity a man finds three things to love: God, himself, and his neighbour. And since he who loves God does not err in his love of himself, it follows that he should counsel his neighbour, whom he is commanded to love as himself, to love God (Aug. ibid., 14).
CLXIII. On concord and obedience.

Domestic peace is the ordered concord in commanding and obeying among those who live together. For those command who take care [of others], as the husband the wife, parents their children, masters their slaves. And those obey who are cared for, as wives their husbands, children their parents, slaves their masters. But in the house of the just man who lives by faith and is still a pilgrim away from that city, even those who command serve those whom they seem to command. For they command not from a desire to dominate but from the duty of caring, not from the pride of ruling but from the kindness of providing (Aug. ibid.).
CLXIV. On the condition of slavery.

Guilt, not nature, gave rise to the name and condition of slavery; and the first cause of this subjection is sin, for, as it is written: Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. Hence the state of one who serves a man is better than that of one who serves his own cupidity (Aug. ibid., 15).
CLXV. On those set over others.

True fathers of families counsel those under them, as sons, to worship God and to earn his favour, desiring to come to the heavenly home where the duty of commanding is not necessary; and until one comes there, the fathers ought [to bear] that they rule more than slaves to endure that they serve (Aug. ibid., 16).
CLXVI. On the governing of a people.

A higher position, without which a people cannot be governed, even if it is to be held and administered as is fitting, is nevertheless unfittingly sought. Hence let love of truth seek holy leisure, and let the necessity of love take up righteous business (Aug. City of God XIX, 19).
CLXVII. On the life of the soul.

Just as what makes the flesh live is not from the flesh but above the flesh, so what makes the soul live blessedly is not from the soul but above the soul; for as the soul is the life of the flesh, so God is the blessed life of man (Aug. ibid., 25).
CLXVIII. On the righteousness of men.

Our righteousness, although it is true on account of the true end of good to which it is referred, is nevertheless such in this life that it consists rather in the forgiveness of sins than in the perfection of virtues (Aug. ibid., 27).
CLXIX. On full peace.

As long as vices are resisted, there is no full peace, for those that resist are subdued in perilous battle, and those that are conquered are not yet triumphed over in secure leisure, but are still held down by an anxious rule (Aug. ibid.).
CLXX. On the first and second death.

The first death drives the unwilling soul out of the body; the second holds the unwilling soul in the body. From both deaths alike this results, that the soul suffers from its own body what it does not want (Aug. City of God XXI, 3).
CLXXI. On the unknown causes of God's works.
In the unknown causes of the divine works we know something when we know that the Almighty does not act without reason in matters of which the weak human mind cannot give a reason (Aug. ibid., 5).
CLXXII. On false confidence.
In vain does a man promise himself after this body what he neglected to acquire in this body (Aug. Enchiridion, 110).
CLXXIII [otherwise CLXXII]. That it profits a man nothing if he does good unwillingly.
No one does good unwillingly, even if what he does is good, for the spirit of fear profits nothing where the spirit of charity is not (Aug. Confessions I, 12).
CLXXIV [otherwise CLXXIII]. On obedience.
Just as among the powers of human society the greater power is placed over the lesser to be obeyed, so God [is placed] over all (Aug. Confessions III, 8).
CLXXV [otherwise CLXXIV]. On true love.

Blessed is he who loves God, and his friend in God, and his enemy for God's sake. For he alone loses no one dear, to whom all are dear in him who is never lost, except by one who forsakes [him] (Aug. Confessions IV, 9).
CLXXVI [otherwise CLXXV]. On things not to be corrupted.

It is evident that things which are corrupted are good: they could not be corrupted if they were highest goods, nor if they were not goods at all; for if they were highest goods they would be incorruptible, but if they were no goods at all, there would be nothing in them to be corrupted (Aug. Confessions VII, 12).
CLXXVII [otherwise CLXXVI]. That God made all creatures good.

Since God, who is unchangeably good, made all creatures good, and no nature at all was created except by him, there is no substance of evil: for what does not have God as its author does not exist. Therefore the vice of corruption is nothing other than the disordered desire or action of the will (Aug. ibid.).
CLXXVIII [otherwise CLXXVII]. That justice is hateful to the wicked.

Just as to an unhealthy palate the food that is pleasant to a healthy one is a torment, and to sick eyes the light in which sound sight rejoices is hateful, so the justice of God displeases the wicked; yet if they submitted to it, they would not be troubled (Aug. ibid., 15).
CLXXIX [otherwise CLXXVIII]. On the sickness of the mind.

It is a sickness of the rational mind when, delighting in lower goods, it partly desires higher things and partly does not desire them. It is therefore divided into two wills; and since each is only one, neither is whole, and what is present to the one is lacking to the other (Aug. Confessions VIII, 9).
CLXXX [otherwise CLXXIX]. On the kind man.

For a kind man it ought to count for little not to stir up or increase others' enmities by speaking ill, unless he also strives to extinguish them by speaking well (Aug. Confessions IX, 9; Celestine I, Letter 1).
CLXXXI [otherwise CLXXX]. On truth that is hated.

The happy life is joy in the truth, which is God; but to many the truth is hateful, and they do not want to hear it when it teaches; and though unwilling to be deceived, they want their own lies to seem to be the truth. They are justly repaid, in that they are not hidden from the truth, but the truth is hidden from them (Aug. Confessions X, 23).
CLXXXII [otherwise CLXXXI]. On endurance.

No one loves what he endures, even if he loves to endure it; for brave patience is one thing and untroubled happiness another, and the toil of battle and the beatitude of victory do not belong to the same time (Aug. ibid., 28).
CLXXXIII [otherwise CLXXXII]. On the poverty of human understanding.
The poverty of human understanding is therefore for the most part copious in speech, because seeking says more than finding, and asking takes longer than obtaining (Aug. Confessions XII, 1).
CLXXXIV [otherwise CLXXXIII]. On the true eternity of God.

True eternity belongs to God, who alone has immortality, because he is changed by no form or movement, nor is his will temporal. For a will that is now one thing and now another is not immortal (Aug. ibid., 11).
CLXXXV [otherwise CLXXXIV]. That sinners are not to be despaired of.

We must not despair of the wicked, but must pray the more earnestly for them, that they may become good; for the number of the saints has always been increased from the number of the ungodly (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 39, 8).
CLXXXVI [otherwise CLXXXV]. How peace is to be sought from God.

Let one who seeks peace from God be at peace with himself, so that there is not one thing in the profession of the mouth and another in the secret of the heart. For it is no use to have in the heart what is true, if what is said with the voice is false; for the truth must both be believed and be spoken (Aug. ibid., 16). CLXXXVII [otherwise CLXXXVI]. That one who is justly scourged should not grieve. Let a man not complain when he suffers some adversities in the things he justly possesses; for through the bitterness of lower things he is taught to love better ones, so that the traveller heading for his homeland may not love the inn in place of his home (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 40, 5).
CLXXXVIII [otherwise CLXXXVII]. That the sinner should be displeasing to himself.
He runs well towards the remission of sins who is displeasing to himself. For before a judge who is just and merciful, he who accuses himself excuses himself (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 41, 12).
CLXXXIX [otherwise CLXXXVIII]. On seeking defences in peace.

The teaching of wisdom must be grasped in the calm of peace, for amid the whirlwinds of tribulation it is recognised only with difficulty. Nor are defences easily found in adversity which were not sought in peace (Aug. ibid., 16).
CXC [otherwise CLXXXIX]. On the twofold altar of God.

To the invisible altar of God, which the unjust does not approach, he attains who approaches this present one justified. For he will find his life there who has here separated his cause (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 42, 5).
CXCI [otherwise CXC]. On the end of the Law.

Christ is the end of the law, in whom the law of righteousness is not used up but fulfilled. For all perfection is in him, beyond whom there is nothing further to which the hope of faith and charity may stretch (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 45, 1).
CXCII [otherwise CXCI]. On the punishment of a bad conscience.

No punishments are heavier than those of a bad conscience: in it, since God is not possessed, no consolation is found; and therefore the deliverer must be called upon, so that the one whom tribulation has driven to confession, confession may lead to pardon (Aug. ibid., 2).
CXCIII [otherwise CXCII]. On the true remission of sins.
What sin of a sick man is graver than the killing of his physician? Yet since this is forgiven in baptism, what is not forgiven (Aug. ibid., 4)?
CXCIV [otherwise CXCIII]. On one who ruminates on the word of God.

The hearer of the word ought to be like the animals which are called clean because they chew the cud: so that he is not slow to think over what he has taken into the belly of his heart; and when he hears, he is like one eating, but when he calls what he has heard back to memory, he is like one chewing the cud (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 46, 1).
CXCV [otherwise CXCIV]. On the rule of the soul.
The rational soul is mistress of its body; but it will not rule the lower well unless it serves the higher, God, in complete subjection of charity (Aug. ibid., 10).
CXCVI [otherwise CXCV]. On the mercy of God.
As the earth awaits rain and light from heaven, so man ought to await mercy and truth from God (Aug. ibid., 15).
CXCVII [otherwise CXCVI]. On the separation of the good and the wicked.

The good sons of the Church should rejoice that divine justice is not deceived in separating them. But let them not rashly divide those who are gathered together: for theirs it is to wish to gather, the Lord's to separate (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 47, 11).
CXCVIII [otherwise CXCVII]. On earthly love.
He is master of the things he has who is ensnared by no cupidity. For he who is bound by love of earthly things does not possess, but is possessed (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 48, sermon 1, 1).
CXCIX [otherwise CXCVIII]. On the eternal inheritance.

The inheritance in which we are co-heirs of Christ is not diminished by the multitude of sons, nor made narrower by the number of co-heirs: but it is as great for many as for few, as great for each as for all (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 49, 2).
CC [otherwise CXCIX]. On happiness.

Happiness ought never to be free of care; for prosperity is more dangerous to the mind than adversity to the body; for prosperity first corrupts, so that adversity may find something to break (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 50, 4).
CCI [otherwise CC]. On the remedies of penance.

The first salvation is to avoid sin; the second is not to despair of pardon. For he destroys himself for ever who, before a merciful judge, does not have recourse to the remedies of penance (Aug. ibid., 5).

CCII [otherwise CCI]. On the hidden goods of the saints. The good are hidden, because their good is in secret; for what they love is neither visible nor bodily, and their merits are set in hiding just as much as their rewards (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 53, 3).
CCIII [otherwise CCII]. On the enemies of the good.

None of the good has an enemy except a wicked one, who is permitted to exist so that he may either be corrected or the good man be exercised through him. We must therefore pray for our enemies, so that either their conversion is obtained or an imitation of the divine goodness is found in us (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 54, 4, and Celestine I, Letter 1).
CCIV [otherwise CCIII]. On the vigour of the Christian faith.

The vigour of the Christian faith is founded at three times: evening, morning and noon. For in the evening the Lord [was] on the cross, in the morning in the resurrection, at noon in the ascension. The first pertains to the patience of the one slain, the second to the life of the one raised, the third to the glory of the majesty of the one seated at the right hand of the Father (Aug. ibid., 18).
CCV [otherwise CCIV]. On the purging of the elect.
Men are harried by tribulations for this purpose: that the vessels of election may be emptied of wickedness and filled with grace (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 55, 13).
CCVI [otherwise CCV]. On the goods which no one loses against his will.
A man can lose temporal goods against his will; but he never loses eternal ones except willingly (Aug. ibid., 19).
CCVII [otherwise CCVI]. On the end of the faithful.

Christ is the end of the faithful: when the striving of the runner has reached him, it has nothing further it could find, but it has that in which it ought to remain (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 56, 2).
CCVIII [otherwise CCVII]. On sadness.
Better is the sadness of one who suffers wrongs than the gladness of one who does wrongs (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 56, 14).
CCIX [otherwise CCVIII]. On past sins.
The mind must be called back from recalling past things with a certain delight, lest, as concupiscence creeps in, we return in heart to Egypt (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 57, 10).
CCX [otherwise CCIX]. On truth.
It is good to be conquered by truth. Let truth overcome a willing man for his correction; for it will overcome even an unwilling one (Aug. ibid., 20).
CCXI [otherwise CCX]. On the impunity of sins.

Sins, whether small or great, cannot go unpunished, because they are punished either by man doing penance or by God avenging. But divine vengeance ceases if human conversion runs ahead of it. For God loves to spare those who confess, and not to judge those who judge themselves (Aug. on Psalm 58, sermon 1, 13).
CCXII [otherwise CCXI]. On the prevenience of God's mercy.
No wretched man is set free from any misery, however great, except one who is anticipated by the mercy of God (Aug. on Psalm 58, sermon 2, 11; canon 14 of the Council of Orange II).
CCXIII [otherwise CCXII]. On the effect of supplication.

One who faithfully entreats God for the needs of this life is both mercifully heard and mercifully not heard. For what is useful to the sick man the physician knows better than the patient. But if he asks for what God both commands and promises, what he asks will certainly be done; for charity receives what truth prepares (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 52, 7).
CCXIV [otherwise CCXIII]. On the advancement of the good through temptations.

The advancement of the faithful does not come about without temptation; nor does anyone come to know himself except by the examination of testing; nor will anyone be crowned except one who has conquered; nor will anyone conquer except one who has fought. And who fights, except one who has an enemy and resists temptation (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 59, 2)?
CCXV [otherwise CCXIV]. On prophecies to be fulfilled.

He is a fool who does not believe the announcements of the prophets in the few things that remain, when he sees so many things fulfilled which did not yet exist when they were foretold as to be fulfilled (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 62, 1).
CCXVI [otherwise CCXV]. On idols.
Those who worship idols are like those who see empty things in dreams. But if their soul wakes up, it understands by whom it was made, and does not worship what it itself made (Aug. ibid., 4).
CCXVII [otherwise CCXVI]. On human bodies.

All the parts of our body which, torn apart, or rotted, or even burned up, are dissolved into a kind of ash, cannot perish to God. For they go into those elements of the world from which they were taken by that hand which holds all things (Aug. ibid., 6).
CCXVIII [otherwise CCXVII]. On good thirst.

Those who thirst for God ought to thirst with their whole substance, that is, both soul and flesh, because God gives to the soul his bread, that is, the word of truth, and God supplies to the flesh what is necessary, because he who made both feeds both (Aug. ibid., 7).
CCXIX [otherwise CCXVIII]. On the meditation of the faithful in leisure and in action.

He who does not think of God when he is at leisure and at rest, how will he be able to think of him amid many activities and laborious business? Let the faithful man therefore meditate on the things of God when he is free, and seek the substance of good working, lest he fail in action (Aug. ibid., 15).
CCXX [otherwise CCXIX]. On the evil of pretence.
Pretended innocence is not innocence; pretended fairness is not fairness; rather the sin is doubled, in which there is both iniquity and pretence (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 63, 11).
CCXXI [otherwise CCXX]. The punishment of the soul that deserts righteousness.

The soul that withdraws from the light of righteousness, the more it seeks what it may find against righteousness, the further it is driven back from the light of truth, and is plunged into darkness (Aug. ibid.).
CCXXII [otherwise CCXXI]. On the two cities.

Two loves make two cities in the whole world: love of God makes Jerusalem; love of the world, Babylon. Let each one therefore ask himself what he loves, and he will find of which [city] he is a citizen (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 64, 2).
CCXXIII [otherwise CCXXII]. That God's commandment is light to one who loves.

Every commandment of God is light to one who loves; nor is it understood to have been said for any other reason, My burden is light (Matt. 11:30), except that he gives the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured out in our hearts (Rom. 5:5), so that by loving we may do freely what one who does it from fear does slavishly; nor is he a friend of what is right when he would prefer, if it were possible, that what is right were not commanded (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 67, 18).
CCXXIV [otherwise CCXXIII]. On charity.

Charity is the fullness of the law, because the law is fulfilled through charity, not through fear (Rom. 13:10). For the commandments of righteousness are done just so far as the spirit of grace helps (Aug. ibid., 24).
CCXXV [otherwise CCXXIV]. On good works.
There are no good works except those which are done through faith and love, because the one without the other brings forth the fruit of no virtue (Aug. ibid., 41; and On the Grace of Christ, ch. 26).
CCXXVI [otherwise CCXXV]. On the fall of Adam and the conversion of the faithful.

Adam was changed from what God formed, but for the worse, through his own iniquity; the faithful are changed from what iniquity wrought, but for the better, through the grace of God. That change therefore was the first transgressor's; this change is of the right hand of the Most High (Aug. on Psalm 68, sermon 1, 2; and canon 15 of the Council of Orange II).
CCXXVII [otherwise CCXXVI]. On temporal delights and punishments.

In the present life both temporal delights are sweet and temporal tribulations are bitter: but who would not drink the cup of tribulation, fearing the fire of Gehenna? And who would not despise the sweetness of the world, longing for the goods of eternal life (Aug. on Psalm 68, sermon 1, 3)?
CCXXVIII [otherwise CCXXVII]. On the Trinity.
In the divine Trinity the unity of substance is so great that it holds equality and does not admit plurality (Aug. ibid., 5).
CCXXIX [otherwise CCXXVIII]. That evil has no nature.

All things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made (John 1:5). Since, therefore, all natures were made through the Word of God, iniquity was not made through him, because iniquity is no substance; and sin is not a nature, but a vice of a nature, desiring what is not of its own order (Aug. ibid.).
CCXXX [otherwise CCXXIX]. What was taken from the devil.

There was taken from the devil, conquered by his own iniquity, not what he had as his own, but what he had seized as another's. For Christ, in taking away the things that had been lost from his great house, did not commit a theft, but recovered a theft (Aug. ibid., 9).
CCXXXI [otherwise CCXXX]. On the depth of iniquity.
The depth of iniquity shuts a man in when he not only lies immersed in sins, but also, wishing to defend them, loses the way of access to confession (Aug. on Psalm 68, sermon 2, 1).
CCXXXII [otherwise CCXXXI]. That God is merciful in tribulations.

When God permits or brings it about that we are troubled by some tribulation, even then he is merciful: because, rousing faith and delaying help, he does not deny aid, but stirs up desire (Aug. ibid.).
CCXXXIII [otherwise CCXXXII]. On rich Christians.

Rich Christians, if they are true Christians, are utterly poor; and in comparison with the heavenly goods which they hope for, they reckon all their gold as sand, because each one has his riches where he has his delight (Aug. ibid., 14).
CCXXXIV [otherwise CCXXXIII]. On the faith of Abraham.
The faith of Abraham is the seed of Abraham. Accordingly, those who belong to the likeness of his believing are the ones who belong to the promise of the heirs (Aug. ibid., 21).
CCXXXV [otherwise CCXXXIV]. On perseverance in good.

Let none of the faithful, however much he has advanced, say, It is enough for me. For whoever has said it has stayed behind and stuck on the way before the end; he will not persevere to the end (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 69, 8).
CCXXXVI [otherwise CCXXXV]. That every place is in God.
There is no place in God, nor is there anywhere to flee from him, except to him. Whoever wishes to escape him offended, let him take refuge in him appeased (Aug. on Psalm 70, sermon 1, 5).
CCXXXVII [otherwise CCXXXVI]. On the two lives.

There are two lives: one is of the body, the other of the soul. As the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul; and just as the body dies if the soul deserts it, so the soul dies if God deserts it (Aug. on Psalm 70, sermon 1, 3).
CCXXXVIII [otherwise CCXXXVII]. From whom it goes well with man.
From whom man has it that he exists, with him he has it that it goes well with him (Aug. ibid., 6).
CCXXXIX [otherwise CCXXXVIII]. On obedience.

God showed perfectly and plainly how great a good obedience is when he forbade man, placed in paradise, a thing which was not evil. There obedience alone could hold the palm; disobedience alone fell into punishment (Aug. ibid., 7).
CCXL [otherwise CCXXXIX]. On the instruction of the good through the wicked.
Sometimes God instructs the good through the wicked, and through the temporal power of those to be damned he exercises the discipline of those to be set free (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 73, 8).
CCXLI [otherwise CCXL]. On confession.
With the mercy of God the confession of the penitent avails very much: the sinner makes him gracious by confessing, whom he does not make ignorant by denying (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 74, 3).
CCXLII [otherwise CCXLI]. That one must not glory in knowledge.
It is the virtue of the humble not to glory in knowledge, because it is common to all; as is the use of light, so is the sharing of truth (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 75, 17).
CCXLIII [otherwise CCXLII]. How bodies are to be ruled.
He does not lack royal power who knows how to command his own body rationally. He is truly lord of the earth who rules his flesh by the laws of discipline (Aug. ibid., 18).
CCXLIV [otherwise CCXLIII]. On him who fears punishment and him who loves justice.

As far as concerns the works that are done outwardly, both he who fears punishment and he who loves justice do not act against the commandment; and so they are equal indeed in hand, but unequal in heart; alike in action, unlike in will (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 77, 11).
CCXLV [otherwise CCXLIV]. What is worshipped.
What a man loves, that he worships. Hence, since God is found greater and better than all things, he is to be loved more than all things, so that he may be worshipped (Aug. ibid., 20).
CCXLVI [otherwise CCXLV]. On the upright heart.
The heart is upright with God when God is sought for God's sake (Aug. ibid., 21).
CCXLVII [otherwise CCXLVI]. On the goodwill of the righteous toward the ungodly.

It comes from goodwill, not from malice, when the righteous man rejoices that vengeance has come upon the ungodly, because what pleases him is not the destruction of the sinner, whom he wished to be corrected, but the justice of God, by which he knows that many can be converted (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 78, 14).
CCXLVIII [otherwise CCXLVII]. On feigning peace with an enemy.
He does not overcome evil with good who is good on the surface and evil in the depths, sparing in deed, raging in heart, gentle in hand, cruel in will (Aug. ibid.).
CCXLIX [otherwise CCXLVIII]. On love and fear.

To every good work love leads, and the fear of God; to every sin love leads, and the fear of the world. So that good may be grasped and evil avoided, one must discern what ought both to be loved and to be feared (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 79, 13).
CCL [otherwise CCXLIX]. Whom misfortune does not break.
No misfortune breaks him whom no good fortune corrupts (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 83, 3).
CCLI [otherwise CCL]. How a rich man is God's poor man.
