A rich man who is such that he despises in himself whatever it is that pride usually swells over is God's poor man (Aug. Expositions on the Psalms 85, 3).
CCLII [otherwise CCLI]. On the steps of devotion.

The affections of devotion are the steps of ascent to God. Your journey is your will: by loving you draw near, by neglecting you draw back; though set on earth you are joined to God, if you love the things that are dear to God (Aug. ibid., 6).
CCLIII [otherwise CCLII]. On petitions contrary to God.
When something is wrongly asked for, God is angry in giving, merciful in not giving (Aug. ibid., 8 and 9).
CCLIV [otherwise CCLIII]. On lying.
It is unbelievable that a man who lies in order to catch [another] does not lie to avoid being caught (Aug. book Against Lying, ch. 4).
CCLV [otherwise CCLIV]. Again on lying.

Although everyone who lies wishes to conceal what is true, yet not everyone who wishes to conceal the truth lies. For often we hide true things not by deceiving but by keeping silent. Nor did the Lord lie when he said (John 16:12), I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now (Aug. ibid., ch. 10).
CCLVI [otherwise CCLV]. On the first and the second man.

In the first man it was shown what the will of man avails for death; in the second, what the help of God avails for life. For the first man was only man; but the second man is God and man. Sin, then, was committed when God was abandoned; righteousness is not done without God (Aug. letter to Dardanus, ch. 9, 30).
CCLVII [otherwise CCLVI]. On the letter of the law.

The letter of the law, which teaches that one must not sin, kills if the life-giving Spirit is absent. For it makes sin known rather than avoided, and so increased rather than diminished, because to evil concupiscence is added also the transgression of the law (Aug. book On the Spirit and the Letter, ch. 5).
CCLVIII [otherwise CCLVII]. On God's commandment and fear.

If God's commandment is done out of fear of punishment, not out of love of justice, it is done slavishly, not freely; and therefore it is not done at all. For that is not good fruit which does not proceed from the root of charity (Aug. ibid., ch. 14).
CCLIX [otherwise CCLVIII]. That the law of God is according to nature.

The law of God is according to nature, and when men do the things of the law, they do them naturally, once the vice has been overcome which not even the defence of the law had removed. So when through grace the law of God is written in hearts (Rom. 2:14), the things of the law are done naturally; not because grace has been forestalled by nature, but because nature has been restored by grace (Aug. ibid., ch. 27).
CCLX [otherwise CCLIX]. On having glory only in God.

Let no one glory in what he seems to have, as if he had not received it; or think that he has received it because the letter appeared outwardly to be read, or sounded to be heard. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing (1 Cor. 4:7; Gal. 2:21). But if he did not die for nothing, Ascending on high he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men (Ps. 67:19). From there has it whoever has it. But whoever denies that he has it from there either does not have it, or what he has will be taken from him (Aug. ibid., ch. 29; canon 16 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCLXI [otherwise CCLX]. What man lost through disobedience.
Man had been made immortal; he wished to be God. He did not lose that he was man, but he lost that he was immortal; and from the pride of disobedience the punishment of [human] nature was contracted.
CCLXII [otherwise CCLXI]. On the praise and reward of faith.
The praise of faith is to believe things not seen; its reward will be to rejoice in attaining the things believed.
CCLXIII [otherwise CCLXII]. Why the Wisdom of God came to men through
the flesh.

Just as milk does not pass except through flesh, to feed the little one who cannot eat bread, so unless the Wisdom of God, which is the bread of angels, had deigned to come to men through the flesh, no one could approach the contemplation of the divinity of the Word. Since, then, the light could not be grasped by the darkness, the light itself underwent the mortality of the darkness, and through the likeness of sinful flesh gave a share in the true light (Aug. on Psalm 33, sermon 1, 6).
CCLXIV [otherwise CCLXIII]. On good reputation.

A good odour is a good reputation; whoever has it through the works of a good life, while following in Christ's footsteps, in a way pours the fragrance of precious ointment over his feet (Aug. On Christian Doctrine 3, ch. 12).
CCLXV [otherwise CCLXIV]. What is rightly loved.
There is no difficulty in going without, except when there is cupidity in having; and therefore that alone is rightly loved which is never well lost (Aug. ibid., ch. 18).
CCLXVI [otherwise CCLXV]. On foolish eloquence.

Whoever overflows with foolish eloquence is the more to be guarded against, the more the hearer is delighted by him in things it is useless to hear, and supposes that one whom he hears speaking ornately is also speaking truly (Aug. On Christian Doctrine, bk. 4, ch. 5).
CCLXVII [otherwise CCLXVI]. On the character of good minds.

It is the evident character of good minds to love the truth in words, not the words, when men discourse. For what use is a golden key, if it cannot open what we want [opened]? Or what harm is there in a wooden one, if it can? Since we seek nothing except that what is shut be opened (Aug. ibid., ch. 11).
CCLXVIII [otherwise CCLXVII]. On loving and not loving the sinner.

No sinner, in so far as he is a sinner, is to be loved; and every human being, in so far as he is a human being, is to be loved for God's sake, but God for his own sake: from whom all who love him have both that they exist and that they love him (Aug. On Christian Doctrine, bk. 1, ch. 27).
CCLXIX [otherwise CCLXVIII]. That the first way to God is Christ.

The Lord says, I am the way, the truth, and the life. That is: through me one comes, to me one arrives, in me one remains. For when one arrives at him, one arrives also at the Father, because he to whom he is equal is known through the one who is equal; the Holy Spirit binding and joining us together, so that we may remain without end in the highest and unchangeable good (Aug. ibid., ch. 34).
CCLXX [otherwise CCLXIX]. That one who is deceived is better than one who lies.

We find many who wish to deceive, but no one who wishes to be deceived. Since one does this knowingly, and the other suffers it unknowingly, it is clear enough that in one and the same matter the one who is deceived is better than the one who lies; since indeed it is better to suffer injustice than to do it (Aug. ibid., ch. 36).
CCLXXI [otherwise CCLXX]. On love of eternal or temporal goods.

Between temporal and eternal things there is this difference: that something temporal is loved more before it is possessed, but grows cheap when it has come; for nothing satisfies the soul except the true and certain eternity of incorruptible joy. But the eternal is loved more ardently when attained than when desired. For no one esteems it more highly than it is in itself, so that it should become cheaper because more was hoped for; rather, so great is its excellence there that charity will attain far more than either faith believed or hope desired (Aug. ibid., ch. 38).
CCLXXII [otherwise CCLXXI]. On spiritual hunger and distaste.

Those who do not find in the holy Scriptures the truth they seek suffer from hunger; but those who do not seek what they have at hand waste away in the languor of distaste; and the danger of both is equal, since blindness withdraws the food of wisdom from the latter and want of it from the former (Aug. On Christian Doctrine, bk. 2, ch. 6).
CCLXXIII [otherwise CCLXXII]. On the labours of the devout.

The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us. Let the world rage and roar, rebuke with tongues, flash with arms: whatever it does, how much will that be beside what we are to receive? I weigh what I suffer against what I hope for; this I feel, that I hope for: and yet what is hoped for is incomparably greater than what is inflicted. Whatever it is that rages against the name of Christ, if it can be overcome, it is bearable; if it cannot, it helps toward reaching the reward more quickly, and the end of temporal evil passes into the receiving of eternal good (Aug. Sermon 279, on the apostle Paul, n. 4).
CCLXXIV [otherwise CCLXXIII]. On charity.

Since the whole Law and the Prophets hang on the two commandments of charity, how much more the Gospel, by which the Law is not abolished but fulfilled, and of which the Lord says, A new commandment I give you, that you love one another (John 13:34)? For charity renews human beings; and as malice makes them old, so love makes them new.
CCLXXV [otherwise CCLXXIV]. On the scourges of God.

When God rebukes the human race and stirs it with the scourges of loving chastisement, he exercises discipline before the judgement, and often loves the one he scourges (Prov. 3:12), not wishing to find one to condemn. He scourges the righteous and the unrighteous together, because there is no one who can boast that he has a chaste heart or that he is clean from sin (Prov. 20:9). Thus even the crowns of the righteous come from the grace of his mercy.
CCLXXVI [otherwise CCLXXV]. On the sufferings of the faithful.

The labour of the devout is training, not condemnation. Nor ought we to be troubled when some holy person suffers grievous and undeserved things, if we have not forgotten what the Righteous One of the righteous and Holy One of the holy endured; whose passion surpasses all passions, because no creature of any kind bears comparison with the author of the universe.
CCLXXVII [otherwise CCLXXVI]. On original sin.

The misery of the human race, from which we see no human being free from birth to death, would not belong to the just judgement of the Almighty if there were no original sin (Aug. Unfinished Work, bk. 1, n. 3).
CCLXXVIII [otherwise CCLXXVII]. On the providence of God at work.

The omnipotence of the all-holding Creator is the cause of subsistence for every creature: and if this power ever ceased from ruling the things it has made, the form and nature of all things would collapse together. Accordingly, what the Lord says, My Father is working until now, shows a certain continuation of his work, by which he at once holds together and administers all things. In this work his wisdom also perseveres, of which it is said, It reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly. The Apostle too holds the same, when, preaching God to the Athenians, he says, In him we live, and move, and are. If he withdrew his work from created things, we could neither live, nor move, nor be. And therefore God is to be understood to have rested from all his works in such a way that he no longer created any nature, not that he ceased to hold together and govern those created (Aug. On Genesis according to the Letter, bk. 4, ch. 12).
CCLXXIX [otherwise CCLXXVIII]. On the observance of the sabbath.

The observance of the sabbath, which was figured by the rest of a single day, having been removed, he keeps a perpetual sabbath who in hope of future rest is intent on holy works, and does not boast of his good acts as if they were his own and not received; recognizing that the one who works in him is he who works and is at rest at once (Aug. ibid., ch. 13).
CCLXXX [otherwise CCLXXIX]. On the rest of God.

The rest of God, for those who understand rightly, is that by which he needs no one's good. And therefore our rest in him is also sure, because we are made blessed by the good which he is, not he by the good which we are. For we too are some good from him, who made all things very good, among which he made us too. Moreover there is no other good thing besides him which he did not make; and therefore he needs no good other than himself, who does not need the good which he made (Aug. ibid., ch. 16).
CCLXXXI [otherwise CCLXXX]. On the beginning of times.

With the motions of the creation once made, times began to run. Hence it is pointless to look for times before the creation, as if times could be found before times. For if there were no motion of spiritual or bodily creation, by which future things succeed past ones through the present, there would be no time at all. But the creation certainly could not move if it did not exist. So time began from the creation rather than the creation from time. But both are from God. For from him, and through him, and in him are all things (Rom. 11:36) (Aug. On Genesis according to the Letter, bk. 5, ch. 5).
CCLXXXII [otherwise CCLXXXI]. That divine Providence rules even the most abject things.

When the Saviour says that not one sparrow falls to the ground without the will of God, and that the grass of the field, soon to be thrown into the oven, he nevertheless forms and clothes (Matt. 10:29; 6:30), does he not confirm that not only this whole part of the world assigned to mortal and corruptible things, but even its vilest and most abject particles are ruled by divine Providence, so that we should not suppose that things whose causes we cannot grasp are disturbed by chance motions (Aug. ibid., ch. 21 and 22)?
CCLXXXIII [otherwise CCLXXXII]. That the rational soul must be raised toward spiritual things.

The rational soul ought to be raised toward those things which most excel in the nature of spiritual things, so that it may savour the things that are above, not those that are on the earth (Aug. Bk. 6 On Genesis to the Letter, ch. 22).
CCLXXXIV [otherwise CCLXXXIII]. That in miracles nothing is done against nature.

God, the founder of natures, does nothing against nature in miracles, nor is what is new to custom repugnant to reason. So unaccustomed things seem against nature to us, to whom the course of nature has become known otherwise; but not to God, for whom nature is whatever he has made (Aug. ibid., ch. 13).
CCLXXXV [otherwise CCLXXXIV]. On the unchangeable plan of the works of God.

It is credible that every body can be changed into every body; but to believe that any body whatever can be turned into a rational soul is absurd. For God is omnipotent in such a way that he never overturns what his own plan has established (Aug. Bk. 7 On Genesis to the Letter, ch. 12 and 20).
CCLXXXVI [otherwise: it was omitted]. That it is natural for us to will to live, but not to live badly.
It is natural for us to will to live; but to live badly is no longer of nature but of a perverse will, which a just punishment follows (Aug. ibid., ch. 27).
CCLXXXVII [otherwise CCLXXXV]. How man is illuminated by the presence of God.

Just as the air has not been made bright by the presence of light, but is being made bright, since if it had been made so and were not being made so, it would remain bright even when the light was absent: so man is illuminated when God is present, but when he is absent is at once darkened; and one departs from him not by distances of place but by the turning away of the will (Aug. Bk. 8 On Genesis to the Letter, ch. 12).
CCLXXXVIII [otherwise CCLXXXVI]. That God must be obeyed.

Great is the benefit to man of serving God when he commands, even when the reason for the command is unknown. For by commanding, God makes useful whatever he wills to command; and there is no need to fear that he may enjoin things that will not profit; nor can it be that a man's own will should not fall upon him with the weight of a great ruin, if in exalting it he sets it above the will of his superior (Aug. ibid., ch. 13).
CCLXXXIX [otherwise CCLXXXVII]. On the excellence of human nature.

How excellent a good human nature is appears most of all from this, that it has been granted to it to be able to cleave to the nature of the highest and unchangeable good. But if it is unwilling, it deprives itself of the good, and this is an evil for it; and from this, through the justice of God, torment also follows. For what is so unjust as that it should go well with a deserter of the good? Sometimes, however, the evil of having lost the higher good is not felt, while the lower good that has been loved is possessed. But it is divine justice that one who by his will has lost what he ought to have loved should lose with pain what he did love, and that the Creator of natures should be praised everywhere. For it is still a good that it grieves at the good it has lost. For unless some good had remained in the nature, there would be no grief for any lost good in the punishment (Aug. ibid., ch. 14).
CCXC [otherwise CCLXXXVIII]. On the power to do harm.

The desire to do harm can be depraved, coming from each person's own mind. But the power is only from God, and that by his hidden and deep justice; for there is no iniquity with God (Aug. Bk. 11 On Genesis to the Letter, ch. 4).
CCXCI [otherwise CCLXXXIX]. How great and what kind of good God is.

How great and what kind of good God is is clearly shown also from this, that it goes well with no one who departs from him: for those who rejoice in deadly pleasures cannot be without fear of pain; and those who, through the greater stupor of pride, do not feel the evil of their desertion at all, are seen by others who know how to discern these things to be weighed down by great misery; so that, if they are unwilling to receive the medicine for avoiding such things, they may serve as an example by which such things can be avoided (Aug. Bk. 11 On Genesis to the Letter, ch. 5).
CCXCII [otherwise CCXC]. That no creature is evil by nature.

Just as true reason teaches that a creature which nothing unlawful delights at all is better, so the same reason teaches that that creature too is good which has it in its power so to restrain unlawful delight that it rejoices not only in the other things lawfully and rightly done, but also in the very restraint of the depraved delight (Aug. ibid., ch. 7).
CCXCIII [otherwise CCXCI]. On the great works of the Lord.

Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills. He foresees those who will be good, and creates them; he foresees those who will be evil, and creates them; offering himself to the good to be enjoyed, bestowing many of his gifts even on the evil; mercifully pardoning, justly punishing; and likewise mercifully punishing, justly pardoning; fearing nothing from anyone's malice; needing nothing from anyone's righteousness; providing nothing for himself from the works of the good, and providing for the good even from the punishments of the evil (Aug. ibid., ch. 11).
CCXCIV [otherwise CCXCII]. On pride and envy.

Since pride is the love of one's own excellence, while envy is hatred of another's happiness, it is plain which springs from which. For each one, by loving his own excellence, envies either his equals, because they are made equal to him; or his inferiors, lest they be made equal to him; or his superiors, because he is not made equal to them. So it is by being proud that one is envious, not by envying that one is proud (Aug. ibid., ch. 14).
CCXCV [otherwise CCXCIII]. How the fullness of the divinity dwells in Christ bodily.

The fullness of the divinity is said to dwell in Christ bodily, not because the divinity is a body, but because the sacraments of the Old Testament are called shadows of what was to come; by comparison with shadows the fullness of the divinity is said to dwell in Christ bodily, because in him all things are fulfilled that were figured in those shadows, and so in a certain way he himself is the body of the preceding shadows, that is, he himself is the truth of those figures and significations (Aug. Bk. 12 On Genesis to the Letter, ch. 7).
CCXCVI [otherwise CCXCIV]. On fighting down vices.

The devout activity in this life is to worship God, and by his grace to fight against inner vices, and not to yield to them when they urge or compel toward unlawful things; and where one does yield, to beg pardon, and, so that one may not yield, God's help, with the affection of religious devotion. But in paradise, if no one had sinned, it would not be an activity of devotion to fight down vices: because the continuance of happiness would consist in not having vices (Aug. Unfinished Work, Bk. 1, n. 70).
CCXCVII [otherwise CCXCV]. On the fortitude of the gentiles and of Christians.

Worldly cupidity produces the fortitude of the gentiles, but the charity of God produces the fortitude of Christians; which has been poured forth in our hearts, not through the choice of the will, which is from us, but through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Aug. ibid., n. 83; can. 18 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCXCVIII [otherwise CCXCVI]. That there is no evil except in some good.
There cannot be any evil except in some good: because it cannot exist except in some nature; and every nature, in so far as it is a nature, is good (Aug. ibid., n. 114).
CCXCIX [otherwise CCXCVII]. That grace is not preceded by any merits.
A reward is owed to good works, if they are done: but grace, which is not owed, goes before so that they may be done (Aug. ibid., n. 133; can. 18 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCC [otherwise CCXCVIII]. On circumcision and baptism.

Circumcision of the flesh was enjoined by the law, because it could not be better signified that original sin is taken away through Christ, the author of regeneration. For every man is born with a foreskin, just as with original sin. And the law enjoined that the flesh be circumcised on the eighth day, because Christ rose again on the Lord's day, which is the eighth after the seventh day, the sabbath. And a circumcised man begets one with a foreskin, passing on to him what he himself already lacked: just as a baptized man nevertheless passes on to the son he begets in the flesh the guilt of origin, from which he himself is already free (Aug. Unfinished Work, Bk. 2, n. 73).
CCCI [otherwise CCXCIX]. On the first and the second man.

The first man, Adam, died long ago, yet in such a way that after him the second man is Christ, although so many thousands of men have arisen between him and the latter; and therefore it is clear that everyone who is born from that succession of descent belongs to the former, just as everyone who is reborn in the latter by the bounty of grace belongs to him. Hence it comes about that the whole human race is in a certain way two men, the first and the second (Aug. Unfinished Work, Bk. 2, n. 163).
CCCII [otherwise CCC]. On the judgements of God.
The judgements of God are in no way to be compared with the judgements of men: there must be no doubt that he is just, even when he does what seems unjust to men (Aug. Unfinished Work, Bk. 3, n. 24).
CCCIII [otherwise CCCI]. On the birth of the righteous.
The righteous man is born of God, not of men: for he becomes righteous by being reborn, not by being born. Hence also the regenerate are called sons of God (Aug. ibid., n. 51).
CCCIV [otherwise CCCII]. On the quality of human nature.

Human nature, although it is bad because it has been vitiated, is nevertheless not an evil, because it is a nature. For no nature, in so far as it is a nature, is an evil, but wholly a good, without which good no evil can exist: for no vice can exist except in some nature; although a nature can exist without vice, either never vitiated or healed (Aug. ibid., n. 206).
CCCV [otherwise CCCIII]. On the death of sinners.

It is the just judgement of God that each should perish by his own sin, though God does not make sin: just as he did not make death, and yet he slays whom he judges worthy of death. Hence we read, God did not make death; and we read, Death and life are from God. That these two are not contrary to each other is surely seen by anyone who distinguishes the divine judgements from the divine works: for it is one thing not to have established [man] mortal in creating him, another to punish the sinner in judging him (Aug. Unfinished Work, Bk. 4, n. 32).
CCCVI [otherwise CCCIV]. On the punishment of sin.

God indeed made the world, and absolutely all bodies. But that the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the flesh lusts against the spirit (Wis. 9:15), is not the antecedent nature of man as established, but the consequent punishment of man as condemned (Aug. ibid., n. 67). CCCVII [otherwise CCCV]. On the good establishment of man.

By however many vices any nature is disfigured, its establishment is always good. For just as the establishment of the body is good even when it is born diseased, and the establishment of the mind is good even when it is born foolish, so the establishment of man himself is good when he is born liable to original sin (Aug. ibid., n. 115).
CCCVIII [otherwise CCCVI]. On the abolition of sin.

Just as some parents aggravate original sin, so some lighten it: but no one takes it away except him of whom it was said, Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world: to whom no good of man is impossible, no evil incurable (Aug. ibid., n. 132).
CCCIX [otherwise CCCVII]. On the grace of God.

It belongs not to the merits of men but to the mercy of God when anyone is set free from that mass of the first man to which death is deservedly owed. For there is no iniquity with God: since he is unjust neither in remitting nor in exacting what is owed; and the pardon is free where the punishment could be just (Aug. Letter 186, to Paulinus, ch. 6, n. 16).
CCCX [otherwise CCCVIII]. That no one is saved except by God's mercy.

Human nature, even if it remained in that integrity in which it was created, would in no way preserve itself without its Creator's help. Hence, since without the grace of God it cannot keep the salvation it received, how can it without the grace of God recover what it has lost (Aug. ibid., ch. 11, n. 37; canon 19 of the Second Council of Orange)?
CCCXI [otherwise CCCIX]. That no excuse is available to the sinner.

Every sinner is without excuse, whether by the guilt of origin or by the addition also of his own will: whether he knows or is ignorant, whether he judges or does not judge. For ignorance itself, in those who refused to understand, is without doubt sin; but in those who could not, it is the punishment of sin. Therefore in both there is not excuse but just condemnation (Aug. Letter 194, to Sixtus, ch. 9, n. 27).
CCCXII [otherwise CCCX]. On those who are led by the Spirit of God.

Beyond doubt it is more to be led than to be ruled. For one who is ruled does something, and is ruled for this purpose, that he may act rightly; but one who is led is understood hardly to do anything himself. And yet the grace of the Saviour grants so much to our wills that the Apostle does not hesitate to say, As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. Nor can free will do anything better in us than commit itself to him who cannot do evil (Aug. On the Proceedings of Pelagius, ch. 3).
CCCXIII [otherwise CCCXI]. What it is to be set free from the body of this death.

To be set free from the body of this death, every infirmity of the concupiscence of the flesh being healed, is to receive the body back not for punishment but for glory (Aug. Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, Bk. 1, ch. 11).
CCCXIV [otherwise CCCXII]. That man can do nothing without God.

God does many good things in man which man does not do; but man does none which God does not cause man to do (Aug. Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, Bk. 2, ch. 8; and canon 20 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCCXV [otherwise CCCXIII]. On true righteousness.

The righteousness according to which the righteous man lives by faith, since it comes to man from God through the spirit of grace, is true righteousness: and although it is not undeservedly called perfect in some righteous people according to the capacity of this life, it is nevertheless small compared with that great one which equality with the angels holds; and he who did not yet have that [righteousness] called himself both perfect, on account of the one which was already present, and imperfect, on account of the other, which was still lacking. But clearly this lesser righteousness makes merit, that greater one makes the reward. Hence one who does not pursue this does not attain that (Aug. Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, Bk. 3, ch. 7).
CCCXVI [otherwise CCCXIV]. That Christ alone, without sin, underwent the punishment of sin.

Concerning the one sole mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, the catholic faith knows that he deigned to undergo death for us, that is, the punishment of sin, without sin. For just as he alone became the son of man for this purpose, that through him we might become sons of God, so he alone took on punishment without evil merits, as we through him [receive] grace without good merits. For just as nothing good was owed to us, so nothing evil was owed to him. Commending therefore his love towards those to whom he was going to give a life not owed, he willed to suffer for them a death not owed (Aug. Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, Bk. 4, ch. 4; canon 2 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCCXVII [otherwise CCCXV]. That grace does not come from nature.

Just as the Apostle says most truly to those who, wishing to be justified in the law, fell away from grace, If righteousness is from the law, then Christ died for nothing (Gal. 2:21), so it is most truly said to those who think that grace, which the faith of Christ commends and receives, is nature: If righteousness is through nature, then Christ died for nothing. For the law was already here, and it did not justify; nature too was already here, and it did not justify. Therefore Christ did not die for nothing: so that both the law might be fulfilled through him who said, I came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matt. 5:17), and nature, lost through Adam, might be restored through him who said that he had come to seek and to save what had perished (Aug. On Grace and Free Will, ch. 15; and canon 21 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCCXVIII [otherwise CCCXVI]. On mercy and judgement.

To be able to have faith, like being able to have charity, belongs to the nature of men; but to have faith, as to have charity, belongs to the grace of the faithful. But since the will to believe is prepared by the Lord for some and not prepared for others, one must distinguish what comes from his mercy and what from his judgement. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10). But his ways are unsearchable (Rom. 11:33). Unsearchable, therefore, are the mercy by which he freely sets free and the truth by which he justly judges (Aug. On the Predestination of the Saints, Bk. 1, ch. 5 and 6).
CCCXIX [otherwise CCCXVII]. On raising up the fallen.
No one raises anyone up to where he himself is unless he descends somewhat to where the other is (Aug. Letter 2, to Nebridius, n. 4).
CCCXX [otherwise CCCXVIII]. On despising the glory of the world.

What power to harm the love of human glory has is felt only by one who has declared war on it. For if it is easy for anyone not to desire praise while it is denied, it is hard not to delight in it when it is offered (Aug. Letter 22, to Aurelius, n. 8).
CCCXXI [otherwise CCCXIX]. On leaving temporal goods behind.

He despises all the riches of the world who despises not only as much as he could have, but also as much as he wished to have. In this one must beware lest pride creep in. For earthly wealth is more profitably held with humility than abandoned with pride (Aug. Letter 31, to Paulinus, n. 5).
CCCXXII [otherwise CCCXX]. On restraining anger.

To no one who is angry does his own anger seem unjust. Hence one must return quickly from all indignation to the gentleness of mildness. For a stubborn emotion easily passes into hatred of the one who is not quickly forgiven (Aug. Letter 38, to Profuturus, n. 2).
CCCXXIII [otherwise CCCXXI]. On law and grace.

He who gave the law also gave grace; but the law he sent through a servant, while with grace he came down himself: so that, since the law shows sins but does not take them away, those who wish to fulfil the law by their own strength, and are not able, may be driven to grace, which takes away both the sickness of incapacity and the guilt of disobedience (Aug. Tractate 3 on the Gospel of John, n. 2).
CCCXXIV [otherwise CCCXXII]. On the sabbath.
The Christian keeps the true sabbath by abstaining from servile work, that is, from sin: since he who commits sin (John 8:34) is the servant of sin (Aug. ibid., n. 19).
CCCXXV [otherwise CCCXXIII]. On the things that are man's own.

No one has anything of his own except falsehood and sin. But if a man has anything of truth and righteousness, it is from that fountain for which we ought to thirst in this desert, so that, sprinkled from it as if with certain drops, we may not faint on the way (Aug. Tractate 5 on John, n. 1; canon 22 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCCXXVI [otherwise CCCXXIV]. On the inseparable working of the Father and the Son.

What the Father does with Christ, Christ does; and what Christ does with the Father, the Father does: nor does the inseparable charity, majesty, power do anything apart, as the Lord himself says (John 10:30): I and the Father are one (Aug. ibid.).
CCCXXVII [otherwise CCCXXV]. To whom the sacrament of baptism is of benefit.

Those who do not keep its gifts do not diminish the grace of regeneration, just as unclean places do not defile the brightness of light. You, then, who rejoice in having received baptism, live in the holiness of the new man; and, holding the faith that works through love, have the good that you do not yet have, so that the good you have may benefit you (Aug. Tractate 6 on John, n. 16).
CCCXXVIII [otherwise CCCXXVI]. How Christ is the truth.

Christ is the truth in such a way that everything in Christ is to be taken as true: true Word of God, God equal to the Father; true soul, true flesh, true man, true God, true birth, true passion, true death, true resurrection. If you call any of these false, rot enters, worms of lies are born from the serpent's venom, and nothing will remain whole; for where there is the corruption of any falsehood, there the wholeness of truth will not be (Aug. Tractate 8 on John, n. 5).
CCCXXIX [otherwise CCCXXVII]. On charity.
How great is charity! If it is lacking, all else is possessed in vain; if it is present, all things are possessed (Aug. Tractate 9 on John, n. 8).
CCCXXX [otherwise CCCXXVIII]. How Christ left his Father and mother.

Christ left his Father, because, being in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6). For this is [what] 'he left the Father' [means]: not that he deserted and withdrew from the Father, but that he did not appear to men in that form in which he is equal to the Father. And he left his mother by leaving the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh, and by cleaving to the Church, which he gathered from all nations.
CCCXXXI [otherwise CCCXXIX]. On the comparison of the first Adam and the second.

Adam sleeps, that Eve may be made; Christ dies, that the Church may be made. From the side of the sleeping Adam Eve is made; when Christ is dead, his side is struck with a lance, so that the sacraments may flow out, by which the Church is to be formed. Hence the Apostle rightly calls Adam himself a figure of the one to come. For as in Adam all die (Rom. 5:14; 1 Cor. 15:22), so also in Christ all shall be made alive (Aug. ibid., n. 10).
CCCXXXII [otherwise CCCXXX]. On the Incarnation of the Word.
God became man: what will man be, for whose sake God became man (Aug. Tractate 10 on John, n. 1)?
CCCXXXIII [otherwise CCCXXXI]. On the two births of men.

One birth is from earth, the other from heaven; one is from flesh, the other from the Spirit; one is from eternity, the other from mortality; one is from male and female, the other from God and the Church. But these two are each single. For as the womb cannot be returned to, so neither can baptism be repeated (Aug. Tractate 11 on John, n. 6).
CCCXXXIV [otherwise CCCXXXII]. On the diversity of goods in God.

If you attend to visible things, bread is not God, water is not God, this light is not God, a garment is not God, a house is not God: for all these are visible, and are separate. For what bread is, water is not; and what a garment is, a house is not; and what these things are, God is not; for they are visible. But God is everything to you that you rightly desire, and the variety of all goods pours forth from one fountain. For when he bestows what is his, he imparts himself under the various names of his gifts (Aug. Tractate 13 on John, n. 5).
CCCXXXV [otherwise CCCXXXIII]. On the soul and the understanding.

The soul that craves carnal things is compared to a woman who has no husband to rule her, namely the understanding, by whose wisdom she ought to be governed: not as though it were something other than the soul, but because it is a certain hidden gaze of the soul. For just as the outer eyes are something of the flesh, so the mind is something of the soul, which excels in it by participation in the divine reason. And then it is well settled in all its movements when it is irradiated by the light from above, so that there may be in it the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world (Aug. Tractate 15 on John, n. 19).
CCCXXXVI [otherwise CCCXXXIV]. On the place of prayer.

You who, about to make supplication to God, seek a fitting and holy place, cleanse your inner parts, and, having driven out from there all evil cupidity, prepare for yourself a secret place in the peace of your heart. Wishing to pray in a temple, pray within yourself; and always act so that you may be a temple of God. For God hears where he dwells (Aug. ibid., n. 25).
CCCXXXVII [otherwise CCCXXXV]. On the senses of the body and the judgement of the mind.

The senses of the body report bodily things to the heart. And the capacity of all is not the same: for one does not see with that by which one hears, nor is smell taken in by that by which taste is; nor are these servants sufficient, without touch, for distinguishing smooth and rough, hot and cold, wet and dry. But the mind judges incorporeal things by its own sense alone, and reaches all their varieties by a single movement; and whatever distinction between good and evil, just and unjust, it rationally discovers is the effect of a single attention: so that the image of God appears there where that by which the mind is able, as far as it is able, is one and the same (Aug. Tractate 18 on John, n. 9 and 10).
CCCXXXVIII [otherwise CCCXXXVI]. On the life of the Son of God.

The Son of God is said to have life in himself, as the Father has, having obtained it not by participation but by being born. For the Father, who is life, begot life; nor does the essence of the begetter and the begotten differ in anything, since the Son is from the Father in such a way that, in co-eternal equality, there is not indeed one person, but one Godhead (Aug. Tractate 19 on John, n. 12 and 13).
CCCXXXIX [otherwise CCCXXXVII]. Why the Son, and not the Father, is said to be the one who will judge.

Although the Father never withdraws from the Son, yet it is not he but the Son who is said to be coming to judge the living and the dead: for there neither the Godhead of the Father nor that of the Son will be seen, but that form of the Son which he united to himself through the sacrament of the incarnation. That form, then, will be judge which stood before a judge; it will judge which was judged; so that the wicked may see the glory of him against whose gentleness they raged. Such a judge, then, will appear as can be seen both by those whom he is to crown and by those whom he is to condemn. But the Father will not appear, since he has not put on the form of a servant; but to the Son, who also became man, he has given the power of judgement (Aug. ibid., n. 16).
CCCXL [otherwise CCCXXXVIII, formerly CCCXXXVI].

How we may do God's will and our own. People do their own will, not God's, when they do what displeases God. But when they do what they will in such a way as to serve the divine will, then, although they do willingly what they do, the will is nonetheless his by whom what they will is both prepared and commanded (Aug. ibid., n. 19; canon 25 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCCXLI [otherwise CCCXXXIX, formerly CCCXXXVII]. On the Father's teaching through the Word.

If the Father teaches the one who hears his word, ask what Christ is, and you will find [that he is] his Word: In the beginning was the Word; not, In the beginning God made the Word, as [it says], In the beginning God made heaven and earth. For the Word of God is God, not a creature; not made among all things, but that through which all things were made. So, in order that a man placed in the flesh might be able to come to the teaching of such a Word, the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (Aug. Tractate 26 on John, n. 8).
CCCXLII [otherwise CCCXL, formerly CCCXXXVIII]. On the flesh of Christ.

The flesh of Christ is the life of the faithful, if they do not neglect to be his body. Let them therefore become the body of Christ, if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ; for nothing lives by it except the body of Christ (Aug. ibid., n. 13).
CCCXLIII [otherwise CCCXLI, formerly CCCXXXIX]. Who eat the body of Christ.

He receives the food of life and drinks the cup of eternity who abides in Christ and in whom Christ dwells. For whoever is at variance with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he receives the sacrament of so great a thing daily and indiscriminately, to the judgement of his presumption (Aug. ibid., n. 18).
CCCXLIV [otherwise CCCXLII, formerly CCCXL]. On the happiness of the wicked.

Worldly wisdom would wish that God never allowed those who are wicked to be happy, which indeed he will not permit; but the wicked are thought happy when they have what they want for this reason, that [people] do not know what happiness is (Aug. Tractate 28 on John, n. 7).
CCCXLV [otherwise CCCXLIII, formerly CCCXLI]. On the change of the heart.

It is one thing to move in body, another in heart. He moves in body who changes place by a motion of the body; he moves in heart who changes affection by a motion of the heart. If you love one thing and used to love another, you are not where you were (Aug. Tractate 32 on John, n. 21).
CCCXLVI [otherwise CCCXLIV, formerly CCCXLII]. On the chrism.

The name of Christ comes from chrism, that is, from anointing. For every Christian is sanctified to this end, that he may understand that he is not only a sharer in priestly and royal dignity, but is also made a wrestler against the devil (Aug. Tractate 33 on John, n. 3).
CCCXLVII [otherwise CCCXLV, formerly CCCXLIII]. On light.

Let us follow Christ the true light, so that we may not walk in darkness. Now the darkness to be feared is that of conduct, not of the eyes; and if of the eyes, not of the outer but of the inner ones, by which is discerned not white and black but just and unjust (Aug. Tractate 35 on John, n. 1).
CCCXLVIII [otherwise CCCXLVI, formerly CCCXLIV]. That Christ is true God and true man.

The Catholic faith believes and proclaims the Lord Jesus Christ to be both true God and true man. For both are written, and both are true. Whoever asserts that Christ is only God denies the medicine by which he was healed. Whoever asserts that Christ is only man denies the power by which he was created. So, faithful and upright soul, accept both: Christ is God, and Christ is man. What kind of God is Christ? Equal to the Father, one with the Father. What kind of man is Christ? The son of a virgin, drawing mortality from man, not drawing iniquity (Aug. Tractate 58 on John, n. 2).
CCCXLIX [otherwise CCCXLVII, formerly CCCXLV]. On the sending of the Word.

The Lord Christ was sent by the Father; he did not withdraw from the Father. His sending was the incarnation, and for the invisible Godhead, to come into this world was the same as to appear. If this were readily grasped, there would be no need for it to be believed, because it would be seen. So by believing is grasped what, unless it is believed, is never understood (Aug. Tractate 38 on John, n. 7).
CCCL [otherwise CCCXLVIII, formerly CCCXLVI]. On faith in the Father and the Son.

To believe rightly about the Father and the Son, the Son himself must be heard, saying, I and the Father are one (John 10:30). For by two words two heresies are cut down at once. By saying "one" he struck down Arius; by saying "are" he laid Sabellius low: for he would neither say "are" of one, nor "one" of what is diverse (Aug. ibid., n. 9).
CCCLI [otherwise CCCXLIX, formerly CCCXLVII]. On Jesus Christ, God and man.

We must know both things in Christ: in what respect he is equal to the Father, and in what respect the Father is greater than he. The one is the Word, the other flesh; the one is God, the other man. But Christ, God and man, is one (Aug. Tractate 37 on John, n. 10).
CCCLII [otherwise CCCL, formerly CCCXLVIII]. On the unity of the divine Trinity.

Many people doubtless have many souls, and there are many hearts; but if they cleave to God through faith and love, they all become one soul and one heart. If, then, the charity of God, which is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5), produces so great a unity of many souls and many hearts, how much more and more surely does an eternal and unchangeable unity remain in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, where the undifferentiated Trinity is one God, one light, and one beginning (Aug. Tractate 39 on John, n. 5)?
CCCLIII [otherwise CCCLI, formerly CCCXLIX]. How the Father taught the Son.

The Father did not teach the Son as though he had begotten him untaught and conferred knowledge on one who did not know; but the timeless teaching is the timeless essence, and to be taught by the Father is the same as to be begotten by the Father: for in the simple nature of truth, to be and to know are not one thing and another, but the very same (Aug. Tractate 40 on John, n. 5).
CCCLIV [otherwise CCCLII, formerly CCCL]. On faith and truth.

Faith always precedes sight. For we believe in order to know; we do not know in order to believe. Faith, then, is to believe what you do not see; truth, to see what you have believed (Aug. ibid., n. 9).
CCCLV [otherwise CCCLIII, formerly CCCLI]. On the good odour of Christ.

The good odour of Christ is the preaching of the truth, from which odour he takes life who serves the Gospel with good conduct and accords with it; but he incurs death whose life disagrees with what he speaks well. This condition also binds the hearers, since right preaching is heard by some, through unbelief, unto death, and received by others, through faith, unto salvation (Aug. Tractate 50 on John, n. 8).
CCCLVI [otherwise CCCLIV, formerly CCCLII]. On the capacity to believe.

The faith of Christ is to believe in him who justifies the ungodly, to believe in the Mediator without whom no one is reconciled to God, to believe in the Saviour who came to seek and save what was lost, to believe in him who said, Without me you can do nothing (John 15:5). But this faith is not grasped by one who, ignorant of the righteousness of God by which the ungodly is justified, wishes to establish his own, by which the proud man is convicted. For those who think such things are hardened and blinded by their own exaltation, since by denying the grace of God they are not helped (Aug. Tractate 53 on John, n. 10).
CCCLVII [otherwise CCCLV, formerly CCCLIII]. On true love.

He who has charity, which comes from a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith, loves God and his neighbour as himself. For the lover of God is the lover of himself; and one who does not love God does not love his neighbour, since he does not love himself. For the sake of this love the hatred of the world too must be patiently endured; for it must needs hate us, whom it sees hating what it loves (Aug. Tractate 87 on John, n. 1 and 2).
CCCLVIII [otherwise CCCLVI, formerly CCCLIV]. On the twofold meaning of "world".

Two kinds of people are called by the one name of world. For as the world is spoken of in the ungodly, so the world is spoken of in the saints. Hence, since the whole of it is at odds with itself in both hatred and love, we are commanded both to hate it and to love it, when we are told, Do not love the world (1 John 2:15), and when we are told, Love your enemies (Matt. 5:44), so that we may desire the salvation of those whose iniquity we abhor (Aug. ibid., n. 4).
CCCLIX [otherwise CCCLVII, formerly CCCLV]. On avoiding glory in knowledge.

For avoiding the temptation of vainglory, the condition of the learner is better than that of the teacher. For truth is more safely heard than preached. Since when teaching is received, humility is guarded; but when disputation gives pleasure, it is hardly possible that some measure of boasting, however small, should not strike the one who discourses (Aug. Tractate 57 on John, n. 2).
CCCLX [otherwise CCCLVIII, formerly CCCLVI]. On the praise with which God proclaims himself.

It is dangerous for a man to please himself, since he must beware of growing proud. But God, however much he praises himself, does not exalt himself, being on high, nor does he wish to seem greater than his own majesty. But when he speaks his power to man, he does not do this so that he himself may become more glorious, but so that man may become better and more learned. For it profits us to acknowledge our maker, and to be subject to him who is above all things, so that concerning him of whom we cannot comprehend what he is, we may not be able to think what he is not (Aug. Tractate 58 on John, n. 3).
CCCLXI [otherwise CCCLIX, formerly CCCLVII]. On forgiving sins.

Christian observance attains to the progress of perfect devotion chiefly through the mutual forgiveness of sins, the Lord giving us the example of his goodness. For if he, in whom there was no sin at all, intercedes for our sins, how much more ought we to pray for one another for our own [sins]? Indeed a man who cannot be free of all sin should embrace so kind a condition, that by forgiving the offences of others he washes away his own (Aug. ibid., n. 5).
CCCLXII [otherwise CCCLX, formerly CCCLVIII]. On the fulfilment of the desires of the righteous.

Nothing will then be lacking to the fulfilment of the desires of the righteous, when God will be all in all of them (1 Cor. 15:28). To this beatitude those attain who die to this world before the separation of the soul from the flesh, and are not found in [the grip of] the cupidities which the love of God alone overcomes: so that iniquity may suffer what it chose, and righteousness may enjoy the good which it loved (Aug. Tractate 65 on John, n. 1).
CCCLXIII [otherwise CCCLXI, formerly CCCLIX]. On confessing Jesus Christ as man.

He who so confesses Christ as God that he denies that he is also true man, that is, having united to himself the nature of our flesh and soul, for him Christ did not die, since Christ died as man. He is not reconciled to God through the Mediator. For there is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5). He is not justified through him, since as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous (Rom. 5:19). He will not rise to the resurrection of life, since through a man [came] death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive (1 Cor. 15:21, 22). Nor let anyone defend himself by the example of blessed Peter, who both accused and washed himself with many tears (Matt. 26:75), so that the Church might follow its chief not by imitation of his denial but of his penance (Aug. Tractate 66 on John, n. 2).
CCCLXIV [otherwise CCCLXII, formerly CCCLX]. On
eternity.

Among certain eternal things there can be some difference, but eternity itself is without diversity of measure. The many mansions indeed signify the various ranks of merits within the one life. But since God will be all in all, there will also be in unequal brightness an equal joy, so that what each has will be common to all. Since through the bond of love no part of the body will be a stranger to the glory of the head (Aug. Tractate 67 on John, n. 2).
CCCLXV [otherwise CCCLXIII, formerly CCCLXI]. On faith.

The faith of those who are to see God believes what it does not see: for if it sees, it is not faith. To the believer merit is gathered; to the one who sees the reward is paid (Aug. Tractate 68 on John, n. 3).
CCCLXVI [otherwise CCCLXIV, formerly CCCLXII]. That God is gracious in not granting the wishes of the wicked.

One who would make bad use of what he wishes to receive does not receive it, rather through God's mercy. Accordingly, if something is asked of him by which a man, if heard, would be harmed, it is rather to be feared that what God could withhold in his favour, he may give in his anger (Aug. Tractate 73 on John, n. 1).
CCCLXVII [otherwise CCCLXV, formerly CCCLXIII]. On Christ's twofold love towards those who love him.

He who loves me, says the Lord, will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him. What does "I will love" mean? As though he were going to love then, and does not love now? Far from it. For how could the Father love us without the Son, or the Son without the Father? How, since they work inseparably, would they love separably? But "I will love" [refers] to what follows, "and I will manifest myself to him"; "I will love, and I will manifest", that is, I will love to this end, that I may manifest [myself]. For now he has loved to this end, that we may believe and hold the commandment of faith; then he will love to this end, that we may see, and receive that very vision as the reward of faith. For we too now love by believing what we shall see; but then we shall love by seeing what we have believed (Aug. Tractate 75 on John, n. 5).
CCCLXVIII [otherwise CCCLXVI, formerly CCCLXIV]. On the vine and the branches of the vine.

The branches are in the vine in such a way that they confer nothing on the vine, but receive from it that by which they live. For the vine is in the branches in such a way that it supplies life-giving nourishment to them, and does not take it from them. And therefore both to have Christ abiding in them and to abide in Christ profits the disciples, not Christ. For when a branch is cut off, another can sprout from the living root; but the one that has been cut off cannot live without the root (Aug. Tractate 81 on John, n. 1; canon 24 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCCLXIX [otherwise CCCLXVII, formerly CCCLXV]. On the measure of human righteousness.

It has been divinely said, Do not be very righteous (Eccles. 7:17). By which is censured not the righteousness of the wise man, but the pride of the presumptuous. He therefore who becomes overly righteous becomes unrighteous by that very excess. But who is it that makes himself overly righteous, if not he who says that he has no sin (Aug. Tractate 95 on John, n. 2)?
CCCLXX [otherwise CCCLXVIII, formerly CCCLXVI]. That the divine substance alone is truly simple.

The substance of no creature, even an incorporeal one, is truly simple, for which to be is not the same as to know; for it can be and not know: but that divine [substance] cannot, since it is the very thing that it has. And therefore it does not have knowledge in such a way that the knowledge by which it knows is one thing and the essence by which it is another, but both are one: although it should not be called "both", since it is most truly simple and one. For the Father has life in himself; and he himself is nothing other than the life which is in him: and he gave the Son to have life in himself; that is, he begot the Son, who should himself also be life. So then we ought to take what was said of the Holy Spirit, For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak (John 16:13), so that we understand that he is not from himself. For the Father alone is not from another. For the Son too is born of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father: but the Father is neither born of another nor proceeds. Yet let no disparity on that account occur to human thought in that supreme Trinity: since both the Son is equal to him of whom he is born, and the Holy Spirit to him from whom he proceeds (Aug. Tractate 99 on John, n. 4).
CCCLXXI [otherwise CCCLXIX, formerly CCCLXVII]. How WAS, and WILL BE, and IS are to be understood in God.

Although the unchangeable nature does not admit "was" and "will be", but only "is": for it truly is, since it cannot be otherwise than it is; yet because of the changeableness of the times in which our mortality and our changeableness move, we say not falsely of him both "was", and "will be", and "is": he was in past ages, is in the present, will be in the future. He was, indeed, because he never was lacking; he will be, because he will never be lacking; he is, because he always is. For he neither perished with things past, as one who now is not; nor slips away with things present, as though he did not abide; nor will arise with things future, as though he had not been. Accordingly, since human speech varies according to the rolling of the times, of him who could not, cannot and will not be able to be lacking through any times, words of any tense are truly said. So the Holy Spirit always hears, because he always knows; and to know and to hear is for him the same as always to be. And for him to be is always to proceed from the Father. But no one can say that the Holy Spirit is not life, since the Father is life and the Son is life. And therefore, just as the Father, since he has life in himself, gave also to the Son to have life in himself, so he gave to him [the Spirit] life, to proceed from him, as he proceeds also from him [the Son] (Aug. Tractate 99 on John, n. 5 and 9).
CCCLXXII [otherwise CCCLXX, formerly CCCLXVIII]. That to love God is a gift of God.

To love God is altogether a gift of God. He who loved us when we did not love him gave [us the power] to love him. We were loved while displeasing [to him], so that there might come to be in us that by which we would please [him]. For the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, whom we love with the Father and the Son, pours charity into our hearts (Aug. Tractate 102 on John, n. 5; canon 25 of the Second Council of Orange).
CCCLXXIII [otherwise CCCLXXI, formerly CCCLXIX]. On the peace of Christ.

The peace of Christ has no end in time, and it is itself the perfection of every devout intention and action. For its sake we are imbued with his sacraments; for its sake we are instructed by his wonderful works and words; for its sake we have received his Spirit as a pledge; for its sake we believe and hope in him, and are kindled with love of him, as far as he grants; for its sake, finally, we bravely endure every tribulation, so that in it we may reign happily without tribulation. For true peace makes unity (1 Cor. 6:17): since he who clings to the Lord is one spirit (Aug. Tractate 104 on John, n. 1).
CCCLXXIV [otherwise CCCLXXII, formerly CCCLXX]. That all time has been ordered by God.

All time has been ordered by him who is not subject to time. For the things that were to come in each several time have their efficient causes in the wisdom of God, in which there are no times. Let us not, then, believe that the hour of the Lord's passion came under the pressure of fate, but rather by God's ordering. For no necessity of the stars brought the cross upon Christ; nor did the stars compel the maker of the stars to die: he who, timeless with the Father, chose the time at which he would die in the flesh, just as [he chose] the manner and the time in which he would be born of his mother (Aug. ibid., n. 2).
CCCLXXV [otherwise CCCLXXIII, formerly CCCLXXI]. On the unity of the Trinity.

In what is said, And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3), the order of the words is: that they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, as the only true God. For the Holy Spirit is understood as following from this. Because he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, as the substantial and consubstantial charity of both. For the Father and the Son are not two gods; nor are the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit three gods; but the Trinity itself is the one only true God. Yet the Father is not the same as the Son; nor is the Son the same as the Father; nor is the Holy Spirit the same as the Father or the Son: since they are three, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit; but the Trinity itself is one God (Aug. Tractate 105 on John, n. 3).
CCCLXXVI [otherwise CCCLXXIV, formerly CCCLXXII]. That the Father gave all things to the Son by begetting [him].

Whatever God the Father gave to God the Son, he gave by begetting. For the Father gave to the Son those things without which the Son could not be the Son in the same way as he gave him to be. For how would he give any words to the Word, in whom he ineffably spoke all things (Aug. Tractate 106 on John, n. 7)?
CCCLXXVII [otherwise CCCLXXV, formerly CCCLXXIII]. On God's keeping of us.

We ought not to take God's keeping of us so carnally, as if the Father and the Son kept us by turns, the keeping of us alternating between the two, as though one took over when the other departed. For the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, who is the one true and blessed God, keep [us] together. But Scripture does not lift us up unless it comes down to us. Just as the Word made flesh came down in order to lift [us] up; it did not fall in order to lie [there]. If we have recognised him coming down, let us rise with him as he lifts [us], and let us understand that when it speaks thus, it distinguishes the persons, not separates the natures.
CCCLXXVIII [otherwise CCCLXXVI, formerly CCCLXXIV]. On the grace of God, by which all merit of man is anticipated.

If we think of the nature in which we were created, since the Truth created all, who is not of the truth? But not all are those to whom it is granted by the Truth itself to hear the truth and to believe, with no merits whatever going before, lest grace be not grace. For if he had said, Everyone who hears my voice is of the truth, he would be thought to be called of the truth because he obeys the truth. But he did not say this; rather, Everyone, he says, who is of the truth hears my voice (John 18:37). And therefore he is not of the truth because he hears its voice; but he hears because he is of the truth, that is, because this gift has been conferred on him by the Truth. And what is this but that, by Christ's gift, he believes in Christ (Aug. Tractate 115 on John, n. 4)?
CCCLXXIX [otherwise CCCLXXVII, formerly CCCLXXV]. On love: we ought to love God.

Whoever loves himself and not God does not love himself; and whoever loves God and not himself, he loves himself. For he who cannot live from himself surely dies by loving himself; so he does not love himself who loves himself so as not to live. But when he is loved from whom one lives, he loves himself the more by not loving himself, who does not love himself precisely in order to love him from whom he lives (Aug. Tractate 123 on John, n. 5).
CCCLXXX [otherwise CCCLXXVIII, formerly CCCLXXVI]. On the undivided work of the Father and the Son.

Whatever it is that the Father must do towards the Son is not done except through the same Son: towards him, that is, because he is the son of man and was made among all things; but through him, because he is the Son of God, and through him all things are made by the Father (Aug. On the Trinity book 1, ch. 7, and Against the Sermon of the Arians ch. 11, n. 9).
CCCLXXXI [otherwise CCCLXXIX, formerly CCCLXXVII]. How the Son will be subject to the Father.

It is not surprising that the Apostle says that the Son will be subject to the Father even in the world to come, where he says, Then he himself also will be subject to him who subjected all things to him (1 Cor. 15:28). For the human form will remain in the Son, in which the Father is always greater. Although there have not been lacking those who thought that this subjection of the Son then is to be understood as a change of that human form into the divine substance, as though each thing were subjected to that into which it is turned and changed; but it is clear that it should be understood that the Apostle said that the Son would be subject to the Father even then rather so that no one should think that the human spirit and body in him were to be consumed by some conversion: so that God may be all, not only in that form of the man, but in all (ibid. 28), when the glory of the head will fill the whole body (Aug. On the Trinity book 1, ch. 8; Against the Sermon of the Arians ch. 27; and Against Maximinus the Arian book 2, ch. 18).
CCCLXXXII [otherwise CCCLXXX, formerly CCCLXXVIII]. That all good things are from God.

All good things, however great, however small, cannot be except from God. For what is greater among creatures than intelligent life? Or what can be less than body? However much these may fail and tend towards not being, yet something of form remains to them, so that they are in some way. And whatever of form remains to any failing thing is from that form which knows not how to fail, and which does not allow the very movements of things failing or advancing to exceed the laws of their numbers. Whatever, therefore, is observed as praiseworthy in the nature of things, whether it is judged worthy of slight or of ample praise, is to be referred to the most excellent and ineffable praise of the Creator (Aug. On Free Choice book 2, ch. 17).
CCCLXXXIII [otherwise CCCLXXXI, formerly CCCLXXIX].

That God's foreknowledge compels no one to sin. God forces no one to sin; yet he foresees those who will sin by their own will. Why then should he not, being just, punish what he, foreknowing, does not force to be done? For just as no one by his memory forces past things to have been done, so God by his foreknowledge does not force future things to be done. And just as a man remembers some things he has done, yet does not do all that he remembers, so God foreknows all things of which he himself is the author, yet is not himself the author of all that he foreknows. And of those things of which he is not the evil author, he is the just avenger (Aug. On Free Choice book 3, ch. 4).
CCCLXXXIV [otherwise CCCLXXXII, formerly CCCLXXX]. On knowing created things that are not seen.

The human soul, being by nature joined to the divine reasons on which it depends, when it says, 'This would be better done than that', if it speaks truly and sees what it says, sees it in those supernal reasons. Let it therefore believe that God has made what by right understanding it has recognised ought to have been made by him, even if it does not see this among the things that have been made. For even if it could not see the heaven with its eyes, and yet by true reasoning gathered that some such thing ought to have been made, it ought to believe that it had been made, although it had not seen it with its eyes. For it would not discern in thought that it ought to have been made, except in those reasons by which all things were made. But what is not there, no one can see by true thought, any more than it is true (Aug. ibid., ch. 5).
CCCLXXXV [otherwise CCCLXXXIII, formerly CCCLXXXI]. By what remedy human wounds are healed.

What is so worthy of mercy as one who is wretched, and what so unworthy of mercy as one who is proud and wretched? Hence it came about that that Word of God, through whom all things were made, and whom all angelic beatitude enjoys, extended his clemency even to our wretchedness, and the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us. For thus man, not yet made equal to the angels, could eat the bread of angels, if the very bread of angels deigned to be made equal to men. Nor did he so descend to us as to desert them; but at once whole for them and whole for us, feeding them inwardly through what God is, admonishing us outwardly through what we are, he makes fit through faith those whom he may feed equally through sight (Aug. ibid., ch. 10).
CCCLXXXVI [otherwise CCCLXXXIV, formerly CCCLXXXII]. That every vice is against nature.

There is no doubt that every vice is against nature, even [the nature] of the thing whose vice it is. Therefore, since in any thing nothing is blamed but vice, and it is a vice precisely because it is against the nature of the thing whose vice it is, the vice of no thing is rightly blamed except of that thing whose nature is praised. For nothing displeases in a vice except that it corrupts what pleases in the nature (Aug. ibid.).
CCCLXXXVII [otherwise CCCLXXXV, formerly CCCLXXXIII]. On the punishment of sin.

For every sinning soul there are two penalties, ignorance and difficulty. From ignorance error deforms it, from difficulty torment afflicts it. But to approve false things as true, so as to err unwillingly, and, with the bond of the flesh resisting and fighting back, to be unable to refrain from unlawful works, is not the nature of man as established, but the punishment of man as condemned (Aug. ibid., ch. 18).
CCCLXXXVIII [otherwise CCCLXXXVI, formerly CCCLXXXIV]. On the variety of remedies.

As the art of medicine, while it remains the same and is in no way itself changed, yet changes its prescriptions for the sick, because our health is changeable; so divine Providence, though itself wholly unchangeable, yet comes to the aid of changeable creation in various ways, and, according to the diversity of diseases, commands or forbids different things to different people: so that it may bring back and make firm, from vice, where death begins, and from death itself, to their own nature and essence those things that are failing, that is, tending to nothing (Aug. On True Religion, ch. 17).
CCCLXXXIX [otherwise CCCLXXXVII, formerly CCCLXXXV]. On the first vice of the soul.

The first vice of the rational soul is the will to do those things which the highest and inmost truth forbids. Thus man was expelled from paradise into this world, that is, from eternal things to temporal, from plenty to want, from strength to weakness. Not, then, from a substantial good to a substantial evil, because no substance is evil; but from an eternal good to a temporal good; from a spiritual good to a carnal good; from an intelligible good to a sensible good; from the highest good to the lowest good. There is therefore a certain good which, if the rational soul loves it, it sins, because it is ranked below it. Therefore the sin itself is evil, not the substance which is loved in sinning (Aug. On True Religion, ch. 20).
CCCXC [otherwise CCCLXXXVIII, formerly CCCLXXXVI]. On the truth that is the law of all arts.

Since the law of all arts is wholly unchangeable, while the human mind, to which it has been granted to see such a law, can suffer the changeableness of error, it is clear enough that above our mind there is a law, which is called truth. Nor now is it to be doubted that the unchangeable nature which is above the rational soul is God; and that the first life and the first essence are there where the first wisdom is. For this is that unchangeable truth which is rightly called the law of all arts, and the art of the almighty Artificer. Therefore, when the soul perceives that it does not judge the form and motion of bodies according to itself, it must at the same time recognise that its own nature excels the nature of which it judges, but that the nature according to which it judges, and of which it can in no way judge, excels itself (Aug., ibid., ch. 30 and 31).
CCCXCI [otherwise CCCLXXXIX, formerly CCCLXXXVII]. By what the heart is stirred to learn.

We are necessarily led to learning in two ways, by authority and by reason. In time authority is prior, but in reality reason. For what is put first in acting is one thing, what is valued more highly in desiring is another. Since, then, the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov. 1:7), and through humility is the step to lofty things, let human ignorance advance through faith, so that faith may merit to see what it believes (Aug. On Order book 2, ch. 9).
CCCXCII [otherwise CCCXC, formerly CCCLXXXVIII]. That one must not be proud of riches, etc.

You flourish in riches, and boast of the nobility of your ancestors, and exult in your homeland, and in the beauty of your body, and in the honours paid to you by men: look at yourself, for you are mortal, and you are earth, and to earth you will go. Look around at those who before you shone with similar splendours. Where are those whom the powers of the citizens courted? Where the invincible emperors? Where those who arranged assemblies and festivals? Where the splendid drivers of horses? The generals of armies, satraps, tyrants? Is not all dust? Is not all ashes? Is not the memory of their life in a few bones? Look at the tombs, and see who is slave, who master, who poor, who rich. Distinguish, if you can, the captive from the king, the strong from the weak, the beautiful from the deformed. Mindful, then, of nature, never be lifted up. And you will be mindful if you look at yourself.
PREFATORY NOTE TO SAINT PROSPER'S BOOK OF EPIGRAMS FROM THE SENTENCES OF SAINT AUGUSTINE.

The hundred and six epigrams, to each of which a theme taken from the selected sentences of Augustine is prefixed, we would judge to be Prosper's from that fact alone. But throughout their whole series our author is so intent on either explaining or defending the doctrines of divine grace, and so accustomed to going back over his earlier conceptions, that by all the features of the work he would betray himself, to be distinguished among thousands, even if all the manuscript codices everywhere, and all the editions and ages, did not show such [an attribution]. This judgement on this work is pronounced in so many words by Joseph Antelmi, so often mentioned, in Dissertation 9, which concerns the poetry of Saint Prosper, among his Critical Dissertations on the works of the Holy Fathers Leo and Prosper.

With what design, or with what fruit, he attempted this, the fair and prudent reader will easily judge, when he understands that the man, intent in all things on the edification of himself and others, aimed at this one thing: that the chief parts of the sentences published in the preceding book should be taken up not only for exercising his poetic vein, but also so that by such a manner of writing they might both cling more tenaciously to the mind and be committed more pleasantly to memory, especially by those to whom the elegance of poems is dear; whose sharpness and force touch men's minds more strongly and also move hearts more effectively, joining true and lasting usefulness to native sweetness, than which nothing is more useful for forming morals, according to that saying of the poet: He has won every vote who has mixed the useful with the sweet.

Or rather, when poetry is taken up for the purpose of teaching spiritual wisdom, it rightly claims for itself on that account what is said of wisdom herself in Wisdom 8:8 [sic], She teaches sobriety and prudence, and justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful for men in life. And below, Her company [wisdom's] has no bitterness, but gladness and joy. And further below still, There is immortality in kinship with wisdom, and good delight in her friendship. All of which truly befit only that wisdom which shines forth in the works of the saints.

That this was his intention in such a work our most holy poet shows clearly enough in the Preface that comes before all the following Epigrams, when he says at the outset: While it pleases [me] to exercise the mind in sacred speech, and it is a delight to feed the soul with heavenly bread.

Whatever is right, however, and whatever may be found there worthy of praise, all of it he wholly wishes to flow back to the heavenly source from which it had flowed, and he takes pains [to show this] again in what follows, singing with the fullest expression of a grateful heart: Nor is this of our own power, but this dew is taken from him who bade the dry rock split open with waters.

Since, moreover, in certain places, that is, in epigrams 65 and 66, Saint Prosper seems to attack the Eutychians, who refused to confess that the body of Christ is consubstantial with our body, when he writes thus: Hence the Word, set into flesh, and the death [he] received, neither confuses itself with the body nor doubles itself. Thus, with heavenly power enlarging the nature of man, so that man might be light in the true light. He who swallowed up the forces of death with a draught of life: what was mortal has been made eternal.

And more pointedly in the following epigram 66: Whoever you are who think things contrary to the eternal counsel, and deny that the Word abides in our flesh, you seek to undo the work of divine devotion, and you desire to rob the world of its hope. For who will save anyone from the wrath to come, or who will be free of the first man's crime, if the Godhead of the Word is not set into our flesh, or Christ was the shadow of a false body? What boy was born from the womb of an untouched Virgin? What nature grew with the years and was increased with food? In what offspring did Abraham believe himself the father of the world? Or what is his stock that sanctifies all things? What race is at once royal and priestly? Or who is at once David's son and Lord, who, as Redeemer, deigned to bring help to those who were slaves of sin and bound with the fetter of death? He who, taking up the flesh of our race together with death, set what is ours against the enemy, so that he might conquer for us. And having put off the flesh he struck down the ruling enemy, so that the ancient prey might win a new palm.

From all these things you may readily conclude that this work was written not long before the time of the Council of Chalcedon, which, as is established, was assembled in the year 451, since it is certain from elsewhere that Saint Prosper survived into the time of this council.
